structure.title: Financial Report > Combined non-financial report
structure.heading: Financial Report > Combined non-financial report
structure.summary:
- The document is KfW Group’s combined non-financial (sustainability) report for FY2024, structured under ESRS and integrating Article 8 EU Taxonomy disclosures, with first-time ESRS application (no prior-year comparatives) and partial ESRS application due to non-integration into the management report.
- It replaces prior GRI and TCFD reporting; topics deemed non-material under ESRS but previously reported will be published separately in 2025.
- Legal and reporting framework: combined non-financial reporting for KfW (parent) and KfW Group per German Commercial Code (HGB); CSRD not yet transposed; scope follows the consolidated financial statements. KfW IPEX-Bank is released from a separate non-financial statement for 2024.
- Basis and standards: coverage of material impacts, risks, and opportunities across the full upstream and downstream value chain; references to IFC Performance Standards, ILO core labour standards, and OECD guidelines; no omissions for IP or pending developments; use of estimates and assumptions disclosed where relevant.
- Quality and assurance: internal controls and risk management processes for sustainability reporting; Deloitte performed independent limited assurance; no external quality assurance beyond this.
- Strategy and materiality: description of business model and value chain; stakeholder interests; integration of sustainability into strategy; assessment of material impacts, risks, and opportunities and their interaction with strategy; materiality assessment processes and determination of material information.
- Governance: roles of the Executive Board and Supervisory Board; sustainability governance structures; due diligence in sustainability matters; internal controls and ESG risk disclosures.
- Environmental topics: overarching targets and actions; SDG mapping of financing; expansion of impact management; environment quota; Environmental and Social Appraisal Guidelines and exclusion lists.
- Climate and energy: greenhouse gas emissions; 1.5°C alignment of financing; Paris-aligned sector guidelines; actions for new financing; DEG climate commitments.
- Pollution and biodiversity: disclosures on pollution; biodiversity actions and policy integration; assessment of climate and biodiversity risks and resilience of strategy and business model.
- EU Taxonomy: legal requirements, methodology, and implementation of taxonomy assessment; group-wide application; detailed disclosures as of 31 December 2024 with supplementary appendix tables.
- Social topics: social matters in operations (diversity and inclusion, remuneration, working conditions, workforce engagement) and in the banking business (value chain workers, affected communities, consumers/end-users, and corporate customers).
- Complaints and grievance mechanisms: group-wide framework including ombudsperson, LkSG procedure, employee channels, and banking business complaints management.
- Business conduct and culture: compliance strategies, corporate culture initiatives, and policies for business conduct.
- Detailed taxonomy KPI tables: GAR assets, sector information, stock and flow KPIs, off-balance-sheet exposures, and templates for nuclear and fossil gas-related activities.
- Independent auditor’s assurance report included at the end.

structure.title: General information
structure.heading: 1 General information
structure.start_phrase:
For financial year 2024, KfW Group’s sustainability reporting is based on a sustainability statement within 
the meaning of the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (“ESRS”; Commission Delegated Regulation [EU] 2023/2772 of 31 July 2023, as amended) for the first time.
structure.summary:
- First-time adoption of ESRS for KfW Group’s 2024 sustainability reporting, prepared in accordance with the EU Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772, with an exception to ESRS 1.110 due to non-integration into the combined management report (partial application).
- ESRS replaces prior reporting frameworks (GRI and TCFD); topics deemed non-material under ESRS but previously reported will be published separately in 2025.
- Includes the combined non-financial report of KfW (parent) and KfW Group in line with HGB Sections 315b, 289b, and 315c in conjunction with 289c–289e, noting CSRD has not yet been transposed into German law.
- Integrates Article 8 EU Taxonomy reporting for 2024.
- Due to first-time ESRS application, quantitative disclosures lack prior-period comparatives (per ESRS 1.136).
- Scope aligns with the consolidated financial statements; covers all entities consolidated under commercial and supervisory law. References to “KfW” mean the parent; “KfW Group” covers all consolidated subsidiaries.
- Annual review of the consolidation scope; this report exempts KfW IPEX-Bank from issuing its own non-financial statement for 2024 under HGB Section 289b(2).
- Where applicable, reporting references other standards and guidelines (IFC Performance Standards, ILO core labour standards, OECD guidelines).
- No omissions were made for intellectual property, know-how, innovation results, or ongoing negotiations.
- Covers material impacts, risks, and opportunities across the entire upstream and downstream value chain; discretionary judgments and assumptions are flagged where used.
- Quality assurance conducted via internal controls and risk management for sustainability reporting; Deloitte performed an independent limited assurance engagement.

structure.title: Basis for preparation of the sustainability report for KfW Group
structure.heading: 2 Basis for preparation of the sustainability report for KfW Group
structure.start_phrase:
In this consolidated sustainability report, the information on sustainability matters of KfW Group is presented 
in accordance with the scope of consolidation of the consolidated financial statements.
structure.summary:
- Scope and framework: For the first time, KfW Group’s 2024 sustainability reporting follows the ESRS (EU Commission Delegated Regulation 2023/2772), with a partial application due to non-integration into the combined management report (exception to ESRS 1.110). ESRS replaces prior GRI and TCFD reporting. Topics deemed non‑material under ESRS but previously reported (GRI/HGB/TCFD) will be published separately in 2025.
- Legal basis and consolidation: The report constitutes the combined non-financial report for KfW (parent) and KfW Group under HGB Sections 315b, 289b and related provisions, as CSRD has not yet been transposed into German law. EU Taxonomy Article 8 reporting for 2024 is integrated. Disclosures follow the consolidated financial statements’ scope; “KfW” refers to the parent only, “KfW Group” includes all consolidated subsidiaries (e.g., KfW IPEX‑Bank, DEG, KfW Capital). The report releases KfW IPEX‑Bank from its individual non‑financial statement requirement for 2024.
- Comparative information: Due to first-time ESRS application, quantitative disclosures do not include prior-period comparatives (ESRS 1.136).
- Standards and completeness: The report references other accepted standards and guidelines where relevant (IFC Performance Standards, ILO core labour standards, OECD guidelines). No omissions were made for intellectual property, know‑how, impending developments, or ongoing negotiations.
- Value chain coverage: Material impacts, risks, and opportunities across KfW Group’s full upstream and downstream value chain are included; discretionary decisions and estimates are flagged where applied. A dedicated section describes the value chain.
- Assurance and controls: Quality assurance follows internal controls and risk management for sustainability reporting; no external QA provider was used. Deloitte conducted an independent limited assurance engagement.
- Time horizons: Disclosures use defined horizons—short term (FY 2024), medium term (up to 5 years), long term (>5 years for impacts; 10+ years for risk/opportunity analysis)—aligned with existing planning and risk processes.
- Incorporation by reference: In line with ESRS 1.119 ff., certain disclosure requirements are fulfilled via cross-references to the combined management report or consolidated financial statements. Referenced topics include business model, economic environment, strategy (Strategic objectives 2029), internal management system, risk management and monitoring, climate/environmental disclosures (E1–E4), social information (S1), and governance (G1).
- Strategy and business model: KfW is a promotional bank owned 80% by the Federal Government and 20% by the federal states, operating under the KfW Law. Its activities include promotional business and Federal Government mandated transactions (which may, in individual cases, deviate from exclusion lists, sector guidelines, and sustainability targets). Products/services span direct financing, on‑lending, and investment across various customer groups. KfW Group reported EUR 21.9 billion in total sales revenue in 2024.

structure.title: Strategy, business model and value chain
structure.heading: 3 Strategy, business model and value chain
structure.start_phrase: KfW as the parent company is a promotional bank of the Federal Republic of Germany.
structure.summary:
- Context and scope: Excerpt from KfW Group’s 2024 Financial Report, Combined non-financial report (General information), with references to ESRS datapoints S1-1 (Strategic objectives 2029), S1-6 (Average number of employees), and G1-1 (Internal control procedures).
- Ownership and mandate: KfW is a state-owned promotional bank (80% Federal Government, 20% federal states) governed by the KfW Law. Activities include promotional business and Federal Government–mandated transactions; mandated transactions may, in justified individual cases, deviate from exclusion lists, sector guidelines, and sustainability/E&S appraisal targets.
- Business sectors and offerings:
  - SME Bank & Private Clients: Promotion of energy efficiency, renewables, sustainability, innovation/digitalisation, general corporate finance, entrepreneurship; education finance (e.g., student loans) and residential housing/energy-efficiency programmes.
  - Customised Finance & Public Clients: Municipal and social enterprise promotion; tailored debt with risk assumption; global financing for banks/leasing firms and state promotional institutions.
  - KfW Capital: Investments in VC and venture debt funds; stakes in coparion and High-Tech Gründerfonds; coordination of Germany’s Future Fund.
  - Export and project finance (KfW IPEX-Bank): International project/export financing for sustainability, digitalisation, infrastructure, raw materials, climate/environmental projects in Germany/Europe’s interests.
  - KfW Development Bank: Public-sector financing in developing and emerging economies across social/economic infrastructure, financial system development, environment/resource protection, migration/displacement, and reforms.
  - DEG: Private-sector development financing in developing/emerging markets, including equity/funds and advisory across agriculture, services, industry, infrastructure/green energy, financial institutions, and PE funds.
  - Note: Financial Markets and Head Office are excluded from the ESRS 2 SBM-1 activity listing.
- Key figure: Total sales revenue of EUR 21.9 billion in 2024.
- Value chain overview:
  - Upstream: Suppliers/service providers (IT, operational services, basic utilities), investors in money/capital markets, and shareholders (Federal Government and federal states).
  - Own operations: Executive Board and Board of Supervisory Directors; workforce across business sectors and central units (HR, Credit Risk Management, Risk Controlling, Compliance, Finance, Group Development & Economics), with some functions managed in subsidiaries.
  - Downstream: Direct financing to corporates, finance companies, public organisations, and private individuals; on-lending via financing partners to end customers; investment via VC/PE funds; liquidity management with market counterparties.
- Funding and credit quality: Capital market funding is material; KfW benefits from institutional liability and a comprehensive Federal Government guarantee (KfW Law Art. 1a), supporting a triple‑A rating; additional federal budget funds are used to channel grants in promotional programmes.
- Value creation: Delivered through internal processes that enable financing solutions and products; business sectors operationalise the model, with cross-references to other report sections for economic environment, business development, and forecasts.

nodes.title: KfW Group’s value chain
nodes.heading: 3.1 KfW Group’s value chain
nodes.start_phrase: KfW Group’s value chain is made up of value chain actors which are part of its own operations or the upstream and downstream value chain.
nodes.summary:
- Defines KfW Group’s value chain across upstream (suppliers, IT/data services, basic utilities; investors in money and capital markets; shareholders), own operations (Executive Board and Supervisory Board; workforce in business sectors and central units like HR, Risk, Compliance, Finance, Economics), and downstream (direct financing, on-lending, investment business, and liquidity management).
- Explains funding model: reliance on capital markets, top-tier AAA ratings supported by institutional liability (Anstaltslast) and comprehensive federal guarantee under Article 1a of the KfW Law; additional federal budget funds for grant programmes.
- Describes own operations as the link enabling internal processes to deliver financing solutions; business sectors execute the model; some functions also organised in subsidiaries.
- Details downstream activities:
  - Direct financing by KfW, KfW IPEX-Bank and DEG for corporates (incl. finance companies), public organisations, and private individuals.
  - On-lending via intermediary financing partners who provide promotional loans; KfW has no direct contractual link to end customers; on-lending is core and legally anchored. E&S Appraisal typically by intermediaries, with KfW oversight/spot checks and exceptions outside EU/OECD high-income; DEG and KfW Development Bank ensure/assess ESMS at intermediaries.
  - Investment business: KfW Capital invests in VC/venture debt funds with ESG due diligence and impact assessment; DEG and KfW Development Bank apply stringent E&S guidelines aligned with IFC Performance Standards and ILO Core Standards.
  - Liquidity managed via a debt securities portfolio.
- Sets value chain boundaries: direct financing ends at first-level partner; on-lending ends at the end customer.
- Outlines broad stakeholder landscape and continuous dialogue across analysts, investors, intermediaries, customers, employees, public sector, NGOs, regulators, media, suppliers, and affected communities/workers.

nodes.title: Interests and views of stakeholders
nodes.heading: 3.2 Interests and views of stakeholders
nodes.start_phrase: As explained in the table below, KfW Group is in continuous dialogue with key stakeholders across its entire value chain.
nodes.summary:
- Governance of investments: DEG’s investments and KfW Development Bank’s fund business follow strict environmental and social (E&S) guidelines, including implementation of E&S management systems, risk categorisation of customers, and implicit adherence to international standards (IFC Performance Standards, ILO Core Labour Standards).
- Stakeholder mapping: KfW Group identifies a broad set of key stakeholders across its value chain, including investors, intermediaries, borrowers, end customers, employees, regulators, policymakers, NGOs, media/research, suppliers, affected communities, and shareholders.
- Stakeholder dialogue formats: Extensive and structured engagement through advisory boards, bilateral talks, investor discussions, networking events, forums, project-site visits, information sessions tied to E&S Appraisals, customer monitoring, NGO dialogues (including at UN climate conferences), political briefings, and corporate advisory boards; each with defined participants, cadence, and purposes.
- Use of engagement results: Dialogue outcomes can enhance formats and feed into strategic planning and operational processes.
- Grievance mechanisms: Group-wide and sector-specific channels for complaints related to human rights and environmental risks, including an LkSG-compliant procedure; multiple options for employee feedback and complaints.
- Internal engagement and oversight: Representation and inclusion of employees in Germany via workers’ representatives, surveys, and internal communications; systematic escalation of stakeholder views to the Executive Board and Board of Supervisory Directors, including reputational risk monitoring.
- Governance bodies and information flow: Regular reporting by the Executive Board to the Board of Supervisory Directors on strategy, risk, compliance, IT, financials, sustainability governance, and key transactions; shareholders exercise control via the Board.
- SME Advisory Council: Legal mandate per KfW Law Article 7a to steer SME promotion, composition and leadership defined by federal ministries and Bundesrat appointees; annual briefings on programmes and ability to request alternatives.
- Strategy integration of sustainability: KfWplus transformation agenda positions KfW as a leading digital transformation and promotional bank, focusing on digitalisation, innovation, climate change mitigation, and biodiversity; operationalised through Strategic objectives 2029.

nodes.title: Integrating sustainability matters into the business strategy
nodes.heading: 3.3 Integrating sustainability matters into the business strategy
nodes.start_phrase: KfW Group believes it has a responsibility to accelerate the sustainable transformation of society and the economy and to boost Germany as an industrial and technological hub.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on structured stakeholder engagement, with adaptable dialogue formats feeding into strategic planning and operations.
- Comprehensive grievance mechanisms for human rights and environmental risks, including sector-specific channels and an LkSG (German Supply Chain Act) complaints procedure; multiple avenues for employees to raise issues.
- Ongoing communication of stakeholder perspectives to the Executive Board and Board of Supervisory Directors, supported by media/NGO monitoring and quarterly reputational risk reviews.
- Active involvement of the Board of Supervisory Directors in governance; regular Executive Board reporting on strategy, risk, compliance, IT, finance, sustainable governance, and significant transactions.
- Description of the SME Advisory Council mandated by the KfW Law: its role in defining the SME Bank mandate, decision-making on SME promotion, annual reporting by the Executive Board, composition, and leadership by the Federal Minister for Economic Affairs and Climate Action.
- Integration of sustainability into business strategy via the KfWplus transformation agenda and Strategic Objectives 2029, targeting leadership in digital transformation and promotional banking, with focus areas including digitalisation, innovation, climate action, and biodiversity.
- Alignment with German federal policies (Climate Action Programme 2030, Sustainable Finance Strategy) and global frameworks (SDGs, Paris Agreement, German Sustainability Strategy); implementation through sector and sustainability guidelines.
- Group-wide sustainable finance approach enhanced by the tranSForm project: impact management tied to SDGs, exclusion lists, E&S appraisal standards, Paris-aligned sector guidelines, and a 1.5°C alignment of financing.
- Introduction of an environmentally sustainable lending definition to meet MaRisk and EBA requirements; tracking an environment quota and a target that SMEs account for more than 40% of new commitments.
- ESG risk management treats ESG as a risk driver affecting financial risks and counterparties’ creditworthiness, with scenario analyses on climate impacts and risk-bearing capacity.
- Strengthened sustainability governance: creation of a Sustainability Strategy division and Chief Sustainability Officer in 2024, integration with Corporate Strategy, and a network of decentralised sustainability officers; target top-three ranking among leading ESG-rated development/promotional banks.
- Human Resources aligned with KfWplus (“top-performing KfW”): talent development, diversity and employer attractiveness, work-life balance, equal opportunity, and upskilling for digital transformation.
- Double materiality assessment covering banking business and operations: material topics include climate change, energy, pollution, biodiversity, value chain workers, affected communities, and consumers/end-users; ESG risks specific to KfW identified, with time-horizon analysis noting a single deviation in energy-related negative impact.

nodes.title: Business model and strategy in the context of material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 3.4 Business model and strategy in the context of material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: In its double materiality assessment, KfW Group has identified various potential and actual impacts, both positive and negative, as well as risks and opportunities.
nodes.summary:
- ESG is treated as a risk driver (not a separate risk type) within KfW Group’s ESG risk management, focusing on the financial effects of environmental, social and governance factors—especially how climate change, social transformation and governance standards affect counterparties’ creditworthiness and KfW’s risk-bearing capacity under different climate scenarios.
- Sustainability governance was strengthened in 2024 with a new Sustainability Strategy division and a Chief Sustainability Officer, integrating Sustainability Policy and Sustainable Finance Management with Corporate Strategy, and supported by a network of decentralised sustainability officers.
- Strategic Objectives 2029 embed sustainability ambition, including targeting an average top‑three ranking among development/promotional banks in a “Best of the Best” peer group across major ESG rating agencies (ISS, MSCI, Sustainalytics).
- Human Resources priorities align with the KfW mandate, business strategy and the KfWplus agenda, emphasizing talent development, employer attractiveness, diversity, work-life balance, equal opportunities and readiness for digital transformation.
- A double materiality assessment identified material impacts, risks and opportunities mainly in the downstream value chain of the banking business; key topics include climate change, energy, pollution, biodiversity, value chain workers, affected communities and consumers/end-users, with time-horizon variation noted only for sub-topic E1 Energy.
- While material impacts, risks and opportunities influence strategy, decisions and the value chain, they have limited effect on the business model due to the KfW Law’s strict framework; they are nonetheless integrated into the Internal Management System.
- Strategy is managed through annual group business sector planning grounded in the KfWplus transformation agenda and Strategic Objectives 2029; sustainability guidelines and an Environmental & Social (E&S) Appraisal seek to identify, avoid, mitigate or offset adverse project impacts.
- Resilience is assessed via annual scenario analyses and stress tests that incorporate ESG risks across multiple time horizons; operational resilience is supported by ESG risk management tools.
- For clarity, material topics are aggregated into four clusters linking them to strategy: Climate and environmental issues in the banking business; Working conditions in banking operations; Persons or groups affected by the banking business; and KfW Group–specific issues, aligned with ESRS sub-topics (climate adaptation/mitigation, energy, pollution, biodiversity).

nodes.title: Assessment of the material impacts, risks and opportunities and their interaction with KfW Group’s strategy
nodes.heading: 3.5 Assessment of the material impacts, risks and opportunities and their interaction with KfW Group’s strategy
nodes.start_phrase: The main impacts, risks and opportunities for KfW Group are presented below.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Explains how material impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) interact with KfW Group’s strategy and value chain. Due to the KfW Law’s strict framework, IROs have limited effect on the business model but are fully embedded in the Internal Management System (IMS) and annual group business sector planning.

- Strategy framework: Strategy is guided by the KfWplus transformation agenda and Strategic Objectives 2029, reviewed annually. Sustainability guidelines and an Environmental & Social (E&S) Appraisal operationalise environmental and social due diligence; exclusion lists and Paris-aligned sector guidelines steer portfolio choices.

- Resilience and risk: Annual scenario analyses and stress tests incorporate ESG risks across time horizons. Risk Controlling uses NGFS and IEA climate scenarios; outcomes inform risk appetite and risk-bearing capacity. Operational resilience is supported by ESG risk tools.

- Climate and environment IROs:  
  - Adaptation: Physical climate risks can increase borrower default risk; financing resilience creates opportunities.  
  - Mitigation: Transition risks affect borrowers; 1.5°C alignment via directing capital to low-carbon investments, with possible mandated exceptions for supply security.  
  - Energy: Strong financing need/opportunity for renewables, efficiency and grid/infrastructure; fossil-related projects may be financed on government mandate.  
  - Pollution: Financing can reduce or contribute to pollution depending on sector.  
  - Biodiversity: Financing can protect or harm ecosystems; a group-wide biodiversity strategy (BioDiv Roadmap) is being developed.

- Strategic anchors: SDG mapping, 1.5°C alignment and an environment quota guide business; climate/environment IROs are continuously monitored and can trigger programme adjustments (e.g., KfW Environmental Protection Programme; oil & gas sector guideline 12/2023).

- Working conditions (banking operations): Only positive impacts identified—better working conditions, non-discriminatory/pay transparency, flexible work, mental health support, inclusive culture. Definitions of employees/non-employees provided; no significant internal risks of child/forced labor; transition plans currently do not impact workforce. Initiatives include an “Employer positioning” project; most benefits accrue to employees in Germany.

- Persons and groups affected by the banking business:  
  - Value chain workers: Financing can create/secure jobs but human rights risks remain, especially in emerging/developing countries; E&S Appraisal applies and case-by-case countermeasures are required.  
  - Affected communities: Financing can improve living conditions (education, health, renewables) but may cause adverse effects (e.g., resettlement, environmental impacts); strict appraisal can lead to avoidance, mitigation, or non-participation. No material risks/opportunities identified.  
  - Consumers/end-users: Positive impacts through non-discriminatory access to finance, housing security, and education funding; delivered directly and via on-lending, aligned with the subsidiarity principle.

- KfW-specific material matters:  
  - Positive impacts: Improved SME access to finance; promotion of sustainable transformation of enterprises and public institutions (targets include >40% SME share; instruments include fees, marketing, environment quota, 1.5°C target, sector guidelines).  
  - Risks: Bank-specific ESG risks across credit/equity (counterparty governance), operational (incl. information security), and compliance (embargoes, bribery, corruption, market manipulation). The “tranSForm” project builds a central ESG risk profile tool and integrates ESG risks into bank-wide processes.

- Materiality assessment: First ESRS 1 double materiality assessment performed for 2024 using 22 ESRS sub-topics plus KfW-specific topics. Conducted via workshops with internal experts, consistency checks, CSO approval, and Executive Board information. Reassessment scheduled annually, next on 30 June 2025.

structure.title: Materiality assessment
structure.heading: 4 Materiality assessment
structure.start_phrase: In order to determine the scope of the sustainability report, KfW Group performed a materiality assessment in accordance with the principle of double materiality as set out in ESRS 1.
structure.summary:
The partial document outlines KfW Group’s approach to promoting SMEs and advancing the sustainable transformation of enterprises and public institutions, aligned with its Strategic Objectives 2029. Key measures include tailored financing and promotional products to address SMEs’ capital-raising disadvantages, sales partner incentives (e.g., upfront fees for microloans), product marketing support, and a target for SMEs to account for over 40% of domestic promotion. Sustainability financing is steered by the environment quota, a 1.5°C alignment target, and Paris‑aligned sector guidelines.

It details the development of ESG risk management via a tranSForm sub-project, creating a central ESG risk profile tool for counterparties, integrating ESG risks into risk instruments and overall bank management, and conducting an ESG risk driver analysis within the risk inventory to support ESRS-aligned materiality.

A comprehensive, ESRS 1 double materiality assessment—performed first for 2024 and to be updated annually—identifies material impacts, risks, and opportunities across KfW, its subsidiaries, and the full value chain. Impacts are scored 0–15 (≥8 material) based on scale, scope, irremediability, and probability; financial materiality for risks/opportunities is scored 0–5 (≥3 material) by magnitude and likelihood, following EFRAG guidance. KfW distinguishes “banking business” from “banking operations,” uses multiple internal/external sources (e.g., exclusion lists, sector guidelines, SDG mapping, ESG risk inventory), and incorporates stakeholder input from 12 groups, including complaint reports and a 2023 interview survey.

Materiality is linked to risk management: ESG risk drivers contributing to material risk types are deemed material and, where not mappable to ESRS, reported under “Banking sector-specific ESG risks.” Governance includes monthly Executive Board risk reporting and regular Supervisory Board updates.

For climate, KfW applies the same process, calculates 2024 GHG emissions for operations and financed portfolios, assesses physical and transition risks at multiple levels (including an in-house tool for counterparties), and uses ESG profiles and stress testing to capture risk materiality and timing.

nodes.title: Processes to identify material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 4.1 Processes to identify material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.summary:
- Explains how KfW Group links its ESG materiality assessment to the enterprise risk inventory, defining ESG risk drivers, estimating their impact on core risk types (e.g., credit, operational), and classifying drivers as material when they contribute to group‑material risks; non‑ESRS‑mappable drivers are reported as “Banking sector‑specific ESG risks.”
- Describes governance and oversight: regular information flows to the Executive Board (monthly risk reports including sustainability) and the Board of Supervisory Directors (at least quarterly), plus ad hoc Executive Board discussions on key sustainability initiatives.
- Details processes to identify material climate‑related impacts, risks and opportunities, including full 2024 GHG accounting for own operations and financed portfolio and expert assessments of KfW’s impacts on climate change.
- Outlines outside‑in climate risk approaches: integration in the risk inventory, an in‑house application to assess business partners’ physical climate risks, and an ESG risk profiling method that considers materiality and time horizons.
- Summarizes climate stress testing:
  - Physical risks: prior drought/social unrest scenario (2023) and a new 2024 flood/heavy rain stress test (results to be reported from FY 2025), modeling location‑based asset damage and effects on PD/LGD and expected loss.
  - Transition risks: long‑term (2024–2050) NGFS scenarios (Net Zero 2050, Disorderly/Delayed Transition, Fragmented World, NDCs) incorporating carbon/energy prices and demand shifts; largest expected‑loss spikes in Net Zero 2050 and Delayed/Disorderly; scenario uncertainty addressed by multi‑scenario analysis; outputs feed business strategy; ongoing focus on long‑term horizons.
  - Short‑term structural scenario (2024–2027) with rapid carbon price increases led by industrialized countries, highlighting impacts on emission‑intensive sectors and macro performance.
- Notes that climate‑related opportunities and risks are embedded in the group‑wide strategy process; the financial report currently uses no climate‑critical assumptions.
- Covers materiality processes for pollution, water and marine resources, biodiversity, and resource use/circular economy across own operations and the value chain, including transition and physical risks for biodiversity (systemic risks and ecosystem services not separately analyzed).
- Finds material negative biodiversity impacts potentially arising from financed activities and possible related community impacts; relies on established complaints channels and analysis of complaint reports; workshop participants considered community perspectives.
- Reports no sites with material pollution; some locations are near biodiversity‑sensitive areas but with no identified negative impacts due to site characteristics and local mitigation plans.
- Lists business activities that may reduce pollution (e.g., environmental protection programmes, development projects, direct financing, venture investments) and those that may finance environmentally harmful/high‑emission sectors, with caveats on programme use, lack of general sector exclusions, and application of Paris‑aligned sector guidelines, exclusion lists, and E&S appraisal guidelines.
- Describes the business conduct materiality process with close involvement of Compliance.
- Concludes that climate change is not material for banking operations (operational emissions are small); financed emissions (Scope 3, category 15) are material. Operational emissions are voluntarily disclosed to keep the GHG footprint complete.
- Explains how material information is determined using defined thresholds, with joint assessments across subsidiaries and consolidated group‑level reporting.
- Provides a mapping of material ESRS disclosure requirements covered (ESRS 2 and ESRS E1: governance, strategy/business model, materiality processes, transition plan, policies, actions and resources) and where they are addressed in the sustainability report, including references to governance structures, risk disclosures, sector guidelines, exclusion lists, impact management, environment quota, and DEG impact/climate commitments.

nodes.title: Determining information identified as material
nodes.heading: 4.2 Determining information identified as material
nodes.summary:
- Scope and structure: Presents an overview of material disclosure requirements for KfW Group’s sustainability report, mapped to ESRS (ESRS 2; E1–E5; S1–S4; G1), distinguishing “Banking operations” and “Banking business,” and indicating where each disclosure is addressed in the report.

- Materiality mapping: Summarizes results of the materiality assessment, identifying which ESRS disclosures are material, not material, or not relevant, including specific climate, biodiversity, pollution, resource use, water, and social disclosures, and where detailed narrative, policies, actions, targets, and metrics appear.

- Integration with EU legislation: Lists datapoints required by other EU regulations (SFDR, Pillar 3, Benchmark Regulation, European Climate Law) that are reported under ESRS 2 or deemed material, noting their materiality status, reporting location, and items not included due to transition periods.

- Climate-related disclosures (ESRS E1): Covers transition plans, policies, actions/resources, targets (including 1.5°C/Paris alignment, sector guidelines, DEG commitments), Scope 1–3 and total GHG emissions and intensity, and anticipated financial effects (with some E1-9 datapoints flagged n/a in 2024).

- Environmental topics beyond climate (ESRS E2–E5): Addresses policies, actions, targets and materiality for pollution, water and marine resources, biodiversity and ecosystems (including resilience, policies on deforestation and oceans, actions, targets, and anticipated financial effects), and resource use/circular economy.

- Social topics (ESRS S1–S4): Details policies, engagement procedures, remediation and grievance mechanisms, actions, targets, and metrics for:
  - Own workforce (diversity and inclusion, remuneration, working conditions, complaints channels, pay gap and compensation metrics).
  - Value chain workers and affected communities (policies, engagement, remediation, targets, grievance mechanisms).
  - Consumers and end-users (policies, engagement, remediation, targets).
  - Human rights commitments, due diligence (UNGPs/OECD, ILO conventions), risks of forced and child labour.

- Governance (ESRS 2 GOV and ESRS G1): Describes roles and responsibilities of KfW’s Executive Board and Board of Supervisory Directors (no general shareholders’ meeting; supervisory board assumes certain shareholder functions), committee structure (Presidial/Nomination, Remuneration, Risk & Credit, Audit), qualification and suitability requirements (per KWG and BaFin), appointment processes, independence, and internal controls/risk management for sustainability reporting.

- Remuneration and incentives: Notes that neither Executive Board nor Board of Supervisory Directors received variable remuneration in 2024; therefore no separate sustainability-linked incentives.

- Board composition and diversity: Provides gender and age distribution for the Executive Board and Board of Supervisory Directors; outlines ongoing training for both boards, including CSRD/ESRS and ESG risk topics.

- Sustainability governance model: Explains enhanced governance with a CSO function within Group Development, CEO accountability for sustainability strategy, CFO responsibility for the sustainability report, and operational implementation via business sector board members and subsidiaries; CSO leads Sustainability Policy and Sustainable Finance Management (including tranSForm, SDG mapping, and Paris alignment) and coordinates a senior management steering body for sustainable finance.

structure.title: Governance
structure.heading: 5 Governance
structure.summary:
- Diversity metrics for KfW’s governing bodies (2024): Executive Board is 50% women/50% men; Supervisory Board is 27% women/73% men; no members of other genders or with missing gender data; majority of members are over 50; ratio of female to male members is 100% on the Executive Board and 37% on the Supervisory Board.
- Targeted governance training: Ongoing training for Executive Board and 37 Supervisory Directors, including courses on sustainability developments, ESG risk management and controlling, and CSRD/ESRS requirements held in Q3–Q4 2024; budget provided for external training.
- Sustainability governance structure: CEO holds overall responsibility for sustainability strategy and communication; CFO is responsible for the sustainability report and, with Executive Board members and subsidiaries, oversees operational implementation for sustainable finance.
- Strengthening of governance in 2024: Establishment of a Chief Sustainability Officer (CSO) function within Group Development to define strategy, coordinate group-wide activities, and act as central contact for the boards; CSO leads Sustainability Policy and Sustainable Finance Management teams, which managed the “tranSForm” project, including SDG mapping and Paris alignment of financing.
- Committees and coordination: The “tranSForm” steering committee served as the senior forum for sustainable finance; from 31 December 2024 its role transitions to the Sustainable Finance Committee (SFC), chaired by the CSO, meeting bi-monthly to involve key business areas and ensure group-wide consistency; the internal Network Sustainable Finance continues with revised name/rules.
- Decentralized execution: Sustainability officers in 15 departments and three subsidiaries (KfW IPEX-Bank, DEG, KfW Capital) act as advisors, coordinators, and contributors to reporting and ESG ratings; annual sustainability programme consolidates action areas, progress, and challenges; units can propose additional targets and actions for banking business and operations.
- Board oversight and due diligence: Executive Board receives an annual overview of material impacts, risks, and opportunities and adjusts targets/actions as needed; Supervisory Board reviews the sustainability report with annual financials each spring and receives ad hoc updates; due diligence anchored in sector and unit sustainability guidelines, including KfW’s human rights policy; Compliance reports annually on LkSG risk assessment.
- Decision-making and controls: Board decisions are based on proposals and discussion, considering alternatives and effects on quantitative control variables such as environment quota, financial metrics (costs/income), risk (RWA budget), and funding needs.
- Due diligence roadmap: The report maps core due diligence elements to specific chapters/sections—governance embedding; stakeholder engagement; identification and assessment of adverse impacts; actions to address impacts (e.g., E&S Appraisal Guidelines, exclusion lists, Paris-aligned sector guidelines, 1.5°C alignment, biodiversity and social measures); and tracking/communication (e.g., ESG risk disclosures, environmental targets, SDG mapping, GHG emissions, DEG Impact/Climate Commitments, customer-related disclosures).

nodes.title: Internal controls and risk management relating to sustainability reporting
nodes.heading: 5.4 Internal controls and risk management relating to sustainability reporting
nodes.start_phrase: Risk management in sustainability reporting is based on the established process-integrated internal control system (“ICS”) of KfW Group.
nodes.summary:
- Describes KfW Group’s sustainability reporting controls as integrated into the existing group-wide internal control system (ICS) and financial reporting processes, enhanced to meet ESRS-specific requirements.
- Explains the ICS risk assessment approach: identification, description, and evaluation via a risk matrix (damage types such as financial, normative, reputational; and probability), with hedging measures documented in a risk control inventory and informed by expert judgment and operational risk data.
- Identifies key sustainability reporting risks around quantitative data (accuracy, completeness, processing) and timeliness, mitigated through multi-stage, decentralized quality assurance and approval processes (including multiple-assessor verification) and leveraging established financial reporting controls.
- Notes that for processes owned outside Finance, risk handling requirements are formalized and published under the “Restructuring sustainability reporting at KfW Group” project.
- States that risk assessment outcomes and controls are incorporated into group ICS rules and reported annually to the Executive Board and the Board of Supervisory Directors, with further detail available in the risk report’s internal control section.
- Clarifies that ESG risks are not a standalone risk category; they act as drivers within existing risk types and are assessed through the risk inventory.
- Highlights key ESG risk drivers: climate risks mainly affect credit risk; counterparty governance affects credit and equity investment risks; KfW’s own governance breaches and information security threats relate to operational risk; demographic change and customer relationship quality impact equity investment risk.
- Outlines a dedicated ESG risk sub-project within the group-wide tranSForm program aimed at enhancing ESG risk identification, assessment, and management and meeting regulatory requirements by end-2024, without an ESRS results-based target.
- Presents the “ESG risk profile” application as the central tool capturing ESG risks of business partners (banks, corporates, funds, securitisations), with country profiles added in H1 2024, and notes the integration of ESG risks into the risk management cycle by end-2024, with further development steps to be detailed in the next section.

nodes.title: Disclosures on ESG risks
nodes.heading: 5.5 Disclosures on ESG risks
nodes.start_phrase: As is the case for all ESG risks, the ESG risks identified as material in the materiality assessment conducted in accordance with ESRS are not classed as an independent category of risk.
nodes.summary:
- Describes KfW Group’s internal controls and risk management for sustainability reporting, building on the group-wide internal control system (ICS) used for financial reporting and enhanced for ESRS-specific needs. It outlines risk identification and assessment via a standardized risk matrix (financial, normative, reputational impacts and probability), documentation in a risk control inventory, and mitigation through multi-stage, decentralized quality assurance and approval (e.g., multiple-assessor verification). Requirements for units outside financial reporting are formalized under the “Restructuring sustainability reporting at KfW Group” project, with outcomes integrated into group ICS and reported annually to the Executive and Supervisory Boards.
- Explains that ESG risks identified as material are treated as risk drivers within existing risk types rather than as a separate category. Climate-related drivers are mainly linked to credit risk; counterparty governance drivers affect credit and equity risks; internal governance breaches and information security relate to operational risk; demographic change and customer relationships affect equity risk. Further detail is referenced in the risk report.
- Details the ESG risk management sub-project within the group-wide “tranSForm” program, aiming (through end-2024) to strengthen ESG risk identification, assessment, and management, and to meet applicable regulatory requirements. The central tool is the ESG risk profile application for business partners (banks, corporates, funds, securitisations, with country profiles added in H1 2024), integrated into the risk management cycle.
- Outlines meta-measures for ESG risk management derived from national and European supervisory guidance: establishing an ESG risk profile database; integrating ESG risks into credit ratings; embedding ESG in risk and business strategies and risk appetite; collateral valuation and risk-bearing capacity; enhancing ESG stress testing; defining/reporting KPIs and KRIs; standard and ad hoc ESG reporting; integrating ESG into the credit process; expanding the ESG risk inventory; specifying operational and reputational ESG risks; assessing market price risk impacts; and increasing external transparency. Group-wide implementation with possible subsidiary-specific actions; planned detailed work packages were completed by end-2024.
- Reports completion (by end-2024) of KPIs for transition, physical, and other climate/environmental risks and related risk appetite, along with ongoing portfolio-level climate risk actions (use of ESG risk profiles and targeted ESG stress tests). Introduces a new group policy, “ESG risk management,” aligning with the 7th MaRisk amendment and the ECB Guide on climate and environmental risks; Risk Controlling will own the policy from 1 January 2025 after tranSForm concludes.
- Introduces the Environmental information chapter linked to KfW’s Strategic Objectives 2029 and the KfWplus transformation agenda, emphasizing sustainability and resilience. Identifies material environmental topics (climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, energy, pollution, biodiversity) and describes overarching targets and actions: SDG mapping of financing, 1.5°C alignment of financing activities, and an environment quota of financing above 38%. The chapter also covers sustainability policies, environmental exclusion lists, topic-specific sections (including GHG emissions, pollution, biodiversity, and material climate/biodiversity risks), and EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures.
- Provides SDG mapping methodology and status: aim to map 100% of annual new business to at least one SDG with disclosure of financing volumes per SDG; comprehensive review at transaction level; in 2024, 98.2% of new commitments were allocated, with a small portion not clearly mappable.

nodes.title: SDG mapping of KfW’s financing activities
nodes.heading: 6.1.1 SDG mapping of KfW’s financing activities
nodes.start_phrase: The United Nations adopted the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development in 2015, covering the three dimensions environmental, social and economic.
nodes.summary:
- The chapter “Environmental information” situates sustainability as a core element of KfW Group’s Strategy 2029 and KfWplus transformation agenda, highlighting climate and environmental aspects under the promotional principles of sustainability, transformation, and resilience.
- A materiality assessment identifies five key topics for the banking business: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, energy, pollution, and biodiversity. The chapter provides overarching targets, actions, and policies, and references topic-specific sections (climate/energy, pollution, biodiversity, and material climate/biodiversity risks) plus EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures.
- Overarching targets:
  - SDG mapping of 100% of annual new business (98.2% achieved in 2024), disclosing financing volumes by SDG.
  - 1.5°C alignment of financing activities (detailed in a separate section).
  - Environment quota of financing of more than 38% of annual new commitments.
- SDG mapping:
  - KfW developed its own approach due to a lack of harmonized indicators, aligning with the UN 2030 Agenda, German federal sustainability strategy, SDG Compass, UN Global Compact, and WBCSD guidance.
  - Mapping uses standard financing data, product/sector classifications, qualitative and quantitative impact indicators, and development markers; negative impacts are mitigated via E&S Appraisal, IFC Performance Standards, and exclusion lists.
  - Illustrative 2024 allocations show substantial volumes for SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities), SDG 7 (Clean Energy), SDG 13 (Climate Action), SDG 9 (Industry/Infrastructure), and SDG 8 (Decent Work; adjusted for mandated energy-stability transactions).
  - Topic linkages: climate/energy contributions primarily to SDG 7 and SDG 13; pollution to SDG 3, SDG 6, SDG 12; biodiversity to SDG 14 and SDG 15, with attention to the mitigation hierarchy and safeguards for indigenous peoples.
  - SDG mapping evidences intended positive contributions but does not quantify overall impact.
- Expansion of group-wide impact management:
  - The “tranSForm” program (through 2024) strengthened governance, impact management, 1.5°C alignment, GHG accounting, ESG risk integration, sustainability reporting, and data/IT.
  - From 2025, Group Development advances harmonized impact indicators (SDG-based), data quality, and automated methodologies for GHG savings (renewables, energy efficiency, transport/mobility), with phased technical implementation.
  - No planned use of biodiversity offsets or similar instruments within impact management; such aspects are handled within E&S Appraisal where needed.
- Environment quota:
  - Target set at a minimum 38% of new commitments; designed to ensure a sustained promotional volume in climate and environmental themes.
  - Eligibility criteria vary by financing type and reflect market norms of public promotional programs; the quota covers material areas of climate mitigation/adaptation, energy, and pollution.
  - Direct inclusion for programs or financings explicitly focused on climate/environment (e.g., renewables, e-mobility, carbon sinks, CCS, production of mitigation/adaptation technologies). Other project or corporate financings require demonstrated resource/emission reductions (e.g., waste, wastewater, air/noise pollution) to qualify.

nodes.title: Expansion of group-wide impact management
nodes.heading: 6.1.2 Expansion of group-wide impact management
nodes.start_phrase: KfW Group’s strategic efforts in the area of “sustainable financing” were grouped in six sub-projects under the “tranSForm” project until the end of financial year 2024.
nodes.summary:
- KfW Group outlines its impact logic from financing to intended outcomes and notes that SDG mapping clarifies contributions but cannot yet quantify sustainability impacts, prompting establishment of a group-wide impact management system.
- The “tranSForm” project (through 2024) expanded sustainable financing with goals to strengthen contributions to the SDGs and Paris climate targets and support a GHG‑neutral future in line with the Federal Government’s mandate, the Climate Action Programme 2030 and the German Sustainable Finance Strategy.
- Key tranSForm elements: governance enhancements, expansion of impact management, 1.5°C alignment of financing, development of a GHG accounting system, tighter integration of ESG risks, implementation of financial sustainability reporting, and data/IT enablement.
- A harmonised, group-wide understanding of impact and SDG-based impact indicators were established; Group Development will continue advancing impact management from 2025.
- 2024 focused on strengthening the data basis (availability and quality) for impact management and on automating existing GHG savings methodologies; centralised technical calculations are being phased in, starting with renewable energy, complementing prior methods for energy efficiency and transport/mobility. Ongoing reporting on methodological advances and indicators is planned.
- Impact measurement is the core of impact management; biodiversity offsets, mitigation actions, and local/indigenous knowledge are not planned tools, but relevant aspects are addressed via Environmental and Social Appraisal when necessary.
- An environment quota is a strategic target within the KfWplus transformation agenda: at least 38% of annual new commitment volume in the reporting year must qualify, defined as eligible new commitments over total new commitments. The self-imposed target ensures sustained climate and environmental promotional activity without stakeholder involvement in its setting.
- Eligibility criteria for the quota vary by financing type and reflect market-standard ambition and public promotional program conditions (no additional scientific input used). The quota covers material areas: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, energy, and pollution.
- Direct inclusion applies to programs with explicit climate/environment focus and to project/corporate financings for renewable energy, e‑mobility, carbon sinks, carbon capture and storage, and production of mitigation/adaptation technologies; in some programs only specific loan purposes qualify.
- Other climate mitigation or pollution-avoidance financings (e.g., waste, wastewater, air/noise control) are included only if specific reduction targets are met with proven resource reductions.

nodes.title: Environment quota
nodes.heading: 6.1.3 Environment quota
nodes.start_phrase: The promotional priority area “climate change and environment” is included as an element in the strategic KfWplus transformation agenda.
nodes.summary:
- Explains KfW Group’s impact logic from financing to outcomes, noting SDG mapping as an initial transparency step that does not yet quantify sustainability impacts.
- Describes the expansion of a group-wide impact management system under the “tranSForm” project to strengthen contributions to the SDGs and Paris climate goals, including governance, 1.5°C alignment, GHG accounting, stricter ESG risk integration, sustainability reporting, and data/IT enablement.
- Notes a harmonised impact understanding and SDG-based impact indicators, with 2024 focused on data availability/quality and technical/procedural upgrades; Group Development assumes ongoing responsibility from 2025.
- Details methodologies for measuring GHG savings (renewables, energy efficiency, transport/mobility), moving toward automated, centralised calculation; initial technical rollout in 2024 for renewables; ongoing methodological reporting planned.
- States impact measurement will not use biodiversity offsets, mitigation actions, or local/indigenous knowledge; such aspects are handled via Environmental and Social (E&S) Appraisals.
- Defines the “environment quota” as a strategic lever in KfWplus, targeting ≥38% of annual new commitments (Strategic Objectives 2029); self-imposed target to sustain high climate/environmental financing.
- Outlines eligibility criteria: direct inclusion for programmes/projects explicitly focused on climate/environment (e.g., renewables, e-mobility, CCS, carbon sinks, adaptation tech); other climate/pollution projects must show ≥15% reduction in resource use/pollution; energy efficiency must deliver ≥15% CO2eq reduction for new investments and ≥20% for replacements; business sectors ensure rule compliance and data quality; methodology unchanged year over year.
- Reports 2024 environment quota of 44% (slightly below 45% prior year, above 38% target). Headwinds: high EU reference rate and state-aid constraints dampened SME Bank & Private Clients and Customised Finance & Public Clients volumes; positives: higher climate/environment shares at KfW Development Bank, Export & Project Finance, DEG, and KfW Capital’s Green Transition Facility.
- Summarises 2024 volumes/quotas by sector (EUR bn; environment quota): Group total 112.8/34.7 (44%); SME Bank & Private Clients 35.8/20.7 (58%); Customised Finance & Public Clients 41.6/1.8 (21%, with adjustments); KfW Capital 1.6/0.1 (4%); Export & Project Finance 23.9/6.6 (28%); KfW Development Bank 7.8/4.7 (60%); DEG 2.5/1.2 (48%).
- Highlights key 2024 programmes contributing to the quota, including:
  - Federal Funding for Efficient Buildings (10.0), Climate-friendly Construction (7.7), Climate Action Campaign for Corporates (1.6), Environmental Protection Programme (0.8) in SME Bank & Private Clients.
  - Development Bank financing in energy/efficiency/urban transport (2.5) and environmental protection incl. biodiversity, water/waste (1.2).
  - Municipal investment loans (0.5), Sustainable Mobility (0.3), Efficient Buildings – Municipalities (0.3), Climate-friendly Construction – Municipalities (0.2), and “Nature-based solutions” (0.2) in Customised Finance & Public Clients.
  - Export & project finance for wind/rail and other energy/mobility (5.0).
  - DEG renewable energy in developing countries (0.4).
  - KfW Capital Green Transition Facility for climate tech funds (0.1).
- Identifies “sustainable transformation” of corporates and public institutions as an overarching topic aligned with SDG contributions, the environment quota, 1.5°C alignment, and Paris-aligned sector guidelines; notes sector-specific roles (e.g., IPEX-Bank focus on renewables/mobility transition; Development Bank’s support across partner-country sectors; DEG’s tailored transformation/climate resilience work; KfW Capital’s climate tech investments).
- Clarifies target governance: environmental targets (SDG contribution, 1.5°C alignment, environment quota) are set annually with the Board of Supervisory Directors for a five-year horizon (from FY 2024), monitored via the internal control system, and adjusted as needed through annual strategic reviews.
- Lists overarching policies on climate, energy, pollution, and biodiversity, including E&S Appraisal guidelines and exclusion lists; policies are embedded in procedural rules, reviewed annually, and assigned clear responsibilities; business-sector guidelines (Development Bank, IPEX-Bank, DEG) operationalise the sustainability mission and E&S standards.

nodes.title: Additional information on KfW Group’s environmental targets
nodes.heading: 6.1.4 Additional information on KfW Group’s environmental targets
nodes.start_phrase: The strategic objectives, including the environmental targets enshrined in them (SDG contribution of KfW’s financing activities, 1.5°C alignment of KfW’s financing activities, environment quota), are defined annually with the Board of Supervisory Directors.
nodes.summary:
- KfW Group designates the sustainable transformation of corporate customers and public institutions as an overarching material topic within climate and environmental management.
- Transformation efforts are aligned with the SDG contribution of financing activities, the environment quota, the 1.5°C target, and Paris-aligned sector guidelines.
- Business sector contributions:
  - Customised Finance & Public Clients and SME Bank & Private Clients: financing for renewable energy, energy efficiency, sustainable mobility, and environmental protection (with commitment volumes referenced elsewhere).
  - KfW Capital: “Green Transition Facility” investing via venture capital funds in start-ups and tech companies driving environmental change.
  - KfW IPEX-Bank: financing projects that enable digital and sustainable business, prioritising renewable energy and mobility transition to support 1.5°C alignment.
  - KfW Development Bank: support in partner countries for renewable energy, environmental protection, sustainable agriculture, education, and health, in collaboration with governments and local stakeholders, aiming for long-term economic, social, and environmental benefits (commitments referenced elsewhere).
  - DEG: tailored transformation support to build sustainable and climate-resilient businesses aligned with the SDGs (with further details in DEG Impact/Climate Commitments).

Policies are integrated into procedural rules, reviewed annually, and have clearly assigned responsibilities in the Organisation Manual.

nodes.title: Overarching policies
nodes.heading: 6.2 Overarching policies
nodes.start_phrase: KfW Group’s overarching policies regarding the topics of climate, energy, pollution and biodiversity are presented in the following chapter.
nodes.summary:
- KfW Group positions the sustainable transformation of corporate customers and public institutions as an overarching material topic, aligned with SDG contribution targets, an environment quota, a 1.5°C financing alignment, and Paris-aligned sector guidelines.
- Business sector contributions:
  - SME Bank & Private Clients and Customised Finance & Public Clients: financing for renewable energy, energy efficiency, sustainable mobility, and environmental protection.
  - KfW Capital: “Green Transition Facility” investing via VC funds in start-ups/tech firms enabling environmental change.
  - KfW IPEX-Bank: focus on digital and sustainable projects, prioritising renewables and mobility transition.
  - KfW Development Bank: supports partner countries across renewables, environmental protection, sustainable agriculture, education, and health with long-term socio-economic-environmental impacts.
  - DEG: works with clients on tailored, climate-resilient transformation aligned with SDGs.
- Environmental targets and governance: strategic objectives (including SDG contribution, 1.5°C alignment, environment quota) are set annually with the Board of Supervisory Directors, apply as “Strategic objectives 2029” from FY 2024 for five years, reviewed annually, and monitored via the internal control system with root-cause analysis for shortfalls.
- Overarching sustainability policies: E&S Appraisal and exclusion lists complemented by topic-specific climate, energy, biodiversity, and ESG risk policies; policies are embedded in procedures, reviewed annually, and have defined responsibilities.
- E&S Appraisal framework:
  - Uses IFC Performance Standards or World Bank ESS, EHS Guidelines, ILO Core Labour Standards, and applicable national standards; sector add-ons include Equator Principles (KfW IPEX-Bank), EDFI standards (DEG), BMZ requirements/human rights strategy (KfW Development Bank).
  - Covers pollution prevention, biodiversity, labour/working conditions, community health/safety, resettlement, indigenous peoples, and cultural heritage.
  - Two-step process: screening/categorisation (A, B+, B, C; FI categories for intermediaries) followed by in-depth assessment for higher-risk projects.
  - Mitigation/offset actions are binding; regular reporting and corrective measures are required; projects with unacceptable residual impacts are not financed.
  - EU/OECD high-income investments primarily benchmark national standards; outside these, both national and international standards apply.
- Domestic promotional business guideline (SME Bank & Private Clients; Customised Finance & Public Clients): uniform E&S framework for direct and on-lending; product-level use-of-proceeds screening informs simplified vs in-depth assessment; actions set for material gaps; partners expected to have proportionate E&S procedures/ESMS; KfW conducts spot checks.
- KfW IPEX-Bank guideline: Equator Principles-based; all financings subject to E&S requirements; independent expert monitoring for category A and B+; contractual reporting; project-level grievance mechanisms and documentation.
- KfW Development Bank guideline: applies to all projects; integrates E&S and climate mainstreaming (mitigation and adaptation) from project inception; aligns with BMZ concepts; embeds sustainability in procurement; requires ESS10-compliant grievance mechanisms; supports E&S documentation via BMZ funds; conducts on-site controls and can mandate third-party monitoring; resettlement/livelihood restoration undergo separate final audits.
- DEG guideline: EDFI/IFC-based E&S due diligence with risk categorisation; project-specific ESAPs for medium/high risks; annual client reporting; internal and external annual audits of process compliance.
- Group-wide exclusion list: bars financing linked to unacceptable climate, environmental, and social risks, including radioactive materials and unbound asbestos, new nuclear power plants (except hazard-reduction for existing assets), uranium mining, upstream coal/oil/gas and associated activities, and projects threatening protected ecosystems without adequate offsets; also excludes activities banned under international conventions (e.g., ozone-depleting substances, CITES-listed species); sets qualitative conditions for palm oil, forestry (RSPO/FSC), and large reservoirs/hydropower.
- KfW Capital exclusion list: extends Group exclusions to oil/gas upstream and midstream, new oil power plants, substantial hazardous chemicals, commercial logging in semi-natural tropical rainforests, non-medical animal testing products, fur-related activities, shark fins, and whaling; compliance ensured through due diligence and contractual terms.
- DEG exclusion list: applies EDFI Harmonised Exclusion List; compliance monitored via DEG’s internal controls; aligns with Group exclusions on pollution and biodiversity.
- Monitoring and accountability across entities: binding action plans, periodic reporting, independent expert reviews where needed, grievance mechanisms, and corrective enforcement ensure ongoing compliance with environmental and social requirements.

nodes.title: Environmental and Social Appraisal Guidelines
nodes.heading: 6.2.1 Environmental and Social Appraisal Guidelines
nodes.summary:
- Scope and purpose: Extract from KfW Group’s 2024 Combined non-financial report (Environmental information) covering exclusions, climate and energy disclosures, financed and operational GHG emissions, 1.5°C alignment and sector guidelines, DEG climate commitments, and biodiversity and pollution topics.

- Exclusion lists:
  - KfW Capital applies an exclusion list (building on KfW Group, IFC and EIF lists) to restrict activities misaligned with ethical, social and environmental standards; compliance is due-diligenced and contractually required.
  - Additional exclusions beyond Group list: upstream/midstream oil and gas (transport/storage), new oil power plants; production/trade of significant quantities of hazardous chemicals; biodiversity-related bans (commercial logging in semi-natural tropical rainforests; non-medical animal testing products, with life-sciences exceptions; fur farming/trade; shark fin and commercial whaling). Social consequences of biodiversity impacts are not separately covered.
  - DEG follows the Harmonised EDFI Exclusion List; implementation is mandatory via E&S appraisal and internal controls.

- Climate and energy: GHG accounting framework
  - First-time 2024 group-wide GHG accounting aligned with ESRS, GHG Protocol (2024 Corporate Standard) and PCAF (Part A).
  - 2024 total gross emissions (market-based): 144,592,421 tCO2e; Scope 1: 3,917; Scope 2 MB: 1,996 (LB: 11,627); significant Scope 3: 144,586,508, mostly Category 15 (investments) at 144,510,150 tCO2e.
  - GHG intensity: 6,601 tCO2e per EUR million net revenue.

- Operational (banking operations) emissions:
  - 2024 total market-based: 82,271 tCO2e across Scope 1, 2 and significant Scope 3 categories (1, 2, 6, 7).
  - German operations purchase 100% green electricity; 86.5% covered by bundled contractual instruments.
  - Emissions calculated using activity data and standard databases (ecoinvent, EEA, USEPA, DEFRA, UBA, IPCC); 7.4% of Scope 3 (excl. Cat. 15) uses primary supplier data.
  - Foreign locations included via extrapolation; results involve estimates and judgments.

- Financed emissions (banking business):
  - Calculated per PCAF across seven asset classes; coverage: 80.1% of total assets.
  - 2024 financed emissions: 144,510,150 tCO2e (Scope 1: 52.84%; Scope 2: 4.54%; Scope 3: 42.62%).
  - Emission concentration: Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply (NACE D) and Transportation and storage (NACE H) together 57.5%; Manufacturing (NACE C) 12.4%.
  - Portfolio economic intensity: 0.331 tCO2e per EUR thousand on EUR 436.8bn financing volume.
  - Data quality: average PCAF Data Quality Score 4.55; 14.1% of financed emissions based on primary reported data; plan to improve data quality and methodology.

- 1.5°C alignment targets and governance:
  - Group sustainability target split into 1) 1.5°C alignment of new financing and 2) portfolio GHG neutrality by mid-century; 2024 set as base year, first progress measurement end-2025.
  - Paris-aligned sector guidelines are the key steering tool; responsibility sits with business sector heads and subsidiary boards; Sustainability Strategy division monitors implementation.

- Paris-aligned sector guidelines:
  - Define science-based, sector-specific minimum requirements for high-emitting sectors, aligned with IEA Net Zero by 2050; balance transformative and transitional technologies while avoiding lock-in.
  - Updated since 2021: strengthened 1.5°C alignment (2022), shipping steered via Poseidon Principles, oil and gas guidelines added in Dec 2023.
  - Applied to new financing with limited exceptions (e.g., federal mandates); embedded in product design, eligibility criteria, contracts, and loan processes across business sectors. KfW Capital currently mostly out of scope but will apply if relevant.

- Actions to achieve 1.5°C alignment:
  - Group-wide GHG accounting built under the tranSForm project to track decarbonisation impacts of sector guidelines.
  - Promotion and financing programs contributing to the environment quota support the transition, subject to refinancing capacity.

- DEG Impact/Climate Commitments:
  - Three commitments (since 2022): enhance development impacts, align with 1.5°C and reduce emissions via a science-based pathway, and support client transformation; target neutral portfolio by 2040 through permanent removals (sink projects).
  - Intensity reduction pathway: average −4.2% per year from 2025 vs. 2021 baseline (413 tCO2e/EUR million), aligned with SBTi absolute contraction; applies to financed emissions from own funds.
  - 2024 actions: climate data-driven customer selection; piloting department carbon budgets (from 2025); client transformation support via CARI and DERa enhancements; investments and guarantees for carbon sink projects; digitised GHG data capture.

- Pollution:
  - Material positive impacts (financing environmental projects) and negative impacts (financing polluting sectors) identified; managed via cross-cutting targets and policies (sustainability guidelines and exclusion lists).

- Biodiversity:
  - Biodiversity roadmap (BioDiv-Roadmap) progressed in 2024 (phase 2): status quo, portfolio/materiality/regulatory/peer analyses, partnership scoping; sets action areas for 2025–2026 to develop and implement a group biodiversity strategy, expand positive-impact projects, reduce negative impacts in new business, manage risks, and begin selective biodiversity data collection.
  - KfW Development Bank focus: EUR 0.5bn in 2024 for projects with biodiversity as primary/secondary objective, OECD DAC biodiversity/tropical forest-labelled.
  - Policies in E&S appraisal: IFC Performance Standard 6 / World Bank ESS6 address habitat loss, fragmentation, invasive species, exploitation, hydrological/nutrient/pollution impacts, endangered species safeguards, ecosystem services; PS7/ESS7 ensure indigenous peoples’ FPIC and social safeguards.
  - Climate-related biodiversity drivers managed via sector guidelines and exclusion lists; no additional group-specific land/ocean/deforestation policies beyond existing E&S guidelines.

- ESG risk perspective:
  - 2024 risk inventory assessed biodiversity risk drivers (e.g., ocean acidification, resource scarcity, dependency on ecosystem services, land/sea use, pollution, species exploitation, resource costs); none deemed material for the year across risk types.

nodes.title: Exclusion lists at KfW Group
nodes.heading: 6.2.2 Exclusion lists at KfW Group
nodes.summary:
- Biodiversity policy framework: KfW applies IFC Performance Standards/World Bank ESS, especially PS6/ESS6, to identify, avoid and minimize biodiversity and ecosystem service impacts (habitat loss/fragmentation, invasive species, exploitation, hydrological changes, nutrient and other pollution), excludes projects that would cause net reductions of endangered species, and requires prevention of invasive species and land degradation. Social dimensions are covered via PS7/ESS7 on Indigenous Peoples (free, prior, informed consent and consultation). No additional KfW-specific policies on land use/agriculture, oceans/seas or deforestation beyond these standards. Climate change as a biodiversity driver is addressed indirectly via climate mainstreaming, ESS6 in KfW Development Bank’s Sustainability Guideline, Paris-aligned sector guidelines, and exclusion lists.

- Climate and biodiversity risk disclosures: General ESG risk management is referenced elsewhere; specific biodiversity risk resilience analysis (FY2024 risk inventory) defined drivers such as ocean acidification, resource scarcity, dependence on ecosystem services, land/sea use, water/soil pollution, animal welfare, species exploitation, and rising resource costs. Potential impacts are mainly through credit and equity risks (higher PDs). A two-step assessment (sector-based screening, then counterparty ESG risk profile with mitigants) found no biodiversity risk drivers material in 2024; stakeholders were not separately included.

- EU Taxonomy context (Article 8): Outlines the EU sustainable finance framework, six environmental objectives, technical screening criteria, and phased reporting. In 2024, financial institutions disclose eligibility for all six objectives and alignment for climate mitigation/adaptation only; full alignment reporting for all objectives begins in 2025. Credit institutions disclose the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) per DDA templates, based on counterparty data, plus qualitative disclosures; banking operations are excluded. Scope is tied to NFRD/CSR-RUG, with CSRD pending transposition as of 31 Dec 2024.

- Application at KfW Group: Sustainability is core to strategy; the “tranSForm” project governs taxonomy implementation. KfW voluntarily publishes group-wide taxonomy KPIs for 2024; KfW IPEX-Bank has reported since 2021 and uses consolidated reporting at group level. KfW supports the taxonomy’s transparency aims but highlights limitations: large portions of its promotional portfolio (sovereigns, supranationals, non-EU counterparties, and SMEs outside NFRD/CSRD) fall outside mandatory screening; the taxonomy’s current focus skews toward climate-related activities; high ambition levels and data gaps depress alignment rates. Consequently, taxonomy results are not yet used to steer business sectors or financing decisions, though selected products reference taxonomy criteria (notably “substantial contribution”).

- Reporting basis and metrics: Taxonomy KPIs use IFRS gross carrying amounts, FinRep classifications for counterparties and product groups, and the regulatory consolidated group consistent with financial consolidation. The GAR measures the share of taxonomy-aligned exposures within covered assets.
