nodes.heading: 6.3.4 Actions to achieve 1.5 °C alignment for new financing
nodes.start_phrase:
As part of the “Paris alignment” sub-project of the “tranSForm” project, a methodology for accounting 
GHG emissions was established to regularly capture the group-wide GHG footprint of the financing portfolio.
nodes.summary:
- KfW Group applies Paris‑aligned sector guidelines to new and extended programmes to ensure alignment with the 1.5°C goal; exceptions may occur when the Federal Republic of Germany mandates financing outside these guidelines.
- Governance and oversight: responsibility for implementing and complying with sector guidelines lies with business sector heads and subsidiary management boards; the Sustainability Strategy division centrally monitors proper implementation.
- Product and loan processes: SME Bank & Private Clients and Customised Finance & Public Clients review and, if needed, adjust product/programme conditions to meet sector guidelines; compliance is embedded in factsheets and contracts as eligibility criteria, with borrowers confirming adherence.
- On‑lending controls: intermediary banks must monitor and document appropriate use of funds per contractual obligations.
- Across Customised Finance & Public Clients, KfW Development Bank, KfW IPEX‑Bank and DEG, each financing is checked and documented for applicability and compliance with sector guidelines; non‑compliant cases cannot proceed.
- KfW Capital’s equity fund‑of‑funds activity is currently outside the scope of sector guidelines but will apply them to new activities or in portfolio reviews if relevant.
- To achieve 1.5°C alignment, KfW is building a group‑wide GHG accounting system (via the “Paris alignment” sub‑project of “tranSForm”) to regularly measure and disclose the portfolio’s financed emissions, accounting for portfolio heterogeneity and improving transparency to stakeholders.
- Additional levers include environment‑quota‑contributing programmes and maintaining ample refinancing capacity to support climate and energy financing.
- DEG’s three Impact/Climate Commitments (since 2022) aim to: increase positive development impact; reduce GHGs in line with a science‑based 1.5°C pathway; and actively support client transformation for resilience and impact.
- DEG’s decarbonisation approach: shift to climate‑conscious new business and offer transformation support to existing clients; permanently remove residual emissions via sink projects from 2040 to achieve a neutral portfolio by 2040; interim targets for 2030/2035 are in development.
- Targets and methodology: reduce portfolio GHG intensity by an average 4.2% annually from 2025 (two‑thirds reduction vs. 2021), measured as tCO2e per EUR million financing cash value; applies to financed emissions per PCAF (Scope 1+2 direct, and Scope 3 cat. 15 for indirect via FIs); 2021 baseline intensity is 413 tCO2e/EUR million.
- Where sector guidelines do not yet cover relevant sectors, DEG applies the SBTi “absolute contraction” 4.2% pathway and, from 2025, department‑specific intensity targets and carbon budgets in screening and final decisions.
- Systems for GHG accounting and progress tracking were tested through 2024; from 2025, DEG will publish performance and progress per ESRS.
- Action hierarchy underpinning DEG’s plan: 1) avoid emissions, 2) reduce emissions and adapt via client transformation pathways, 3) neutralise remaining emissions from 2040, collectively targeting a 4.2% annual portfolio intensity reduction from 2025.

nodes.title: DEG Impact/Climate Commitments
nodes.heading: 6.3.5 DEG Impact/Climate Commitments
nodes.start_phrase:
With the adoption of the three Impact/Climate Commitments, DEG’s work since 2022 has focused (1) in an even more targeted manner on further increasing the positive development impacts of its customers’ 
projects on society and the environment, (2) reducing greenhouse gas emissions in line with the Paris Climate 
Agreement’s 1.5° C target in the fight against climate change using a science-based pathway and 
(3) actively supporting its customers in their transformation to strengthen their resilience and achieve even 
greater development impacts.
nodes.summary:
- The section outlines DEG’s three Impact/Climate Commitments: maximizing positive development impacts, reducing GHGs in line with the Paris 1.5°C goal via a science-based pathway, and actively supporting customer transformation and resilience.
- DEG’s climate strategy centers on decarbonizing its portfolio through climate-conscious new business (avoidance), transformation support for existing clients (reduction), and permanent removal of residual emissions from 2040 via carbon sink investments to achieve a climate-neutral portfolio by 2040; an investment strategy and interim 2030/2035 targets are being developed.
- Target framework: reduce portfolio GHG intensity by an average 4.2% annually from 2025 versus 2021 (aiming for a two-thirds reduction), measured as t CO2e per EUR million financing cash value for ordinary business financed with own funds; coverage includes financed emissions per PCAF (Scope 1 and 2 in direct financing; attributable Scope 3 cat. 15 for indirect FI financing) and excludes emissions from on-lending of external funds.
- Governance and methodology: alignment with Paris-aligned sector guidelines, SBTi requirements (absolute contraction approach for mixed portfolios), and MDB Principles for Paris Alignment; department-level emission intensity targets and carbon budgets will guide early assessment and final financing decisions from 2025.
- Baseline and systems: 2021 baseline GHG intensity is 413 t CO2e per EUR million; full financed-emissions accounting established using customer data and GHG modeling; a test phase through 2024 built the GHG accounting and progress measurement systems, with ESRS-aligned performance reporting to start in 2025.
- Key actions to achieve targets:
  - Climate-friendly customer selection (avoidance): pre-commitment climate data collection and Paris alignment checks; introduce carbon budgets for direct business from 2025.
  - Management of new business (reduction): define and pilot department-specific carbon budgets (Corporates and Infrastructure) from 2025 to enable and steer higher-emitter transformations.
  - Transformation support (reduction and adaptation): scale advisory via the CARI program; integrate CO2e reduction/transformation into the DERa framework with a 2024 portfolio score target of 32.
  - Neutralisation (from 2040): build a diversified afforestation/reforestation sink portfolio to remove remaining financed emissions.
- 2024 progress highlights: expanded climate management/advisory HR capacity; digitized portfolio customer GHG data collection and integration; delivered climate-relevant Business Support (e.g., fund carbon accounting training, bank GHG inventory modeling) and pilot advisory with clients in Nicaragua and Nigeria; contributed EUR 1.5 million to DEG Impulse’s CARI; invested in another carbon sink fund and secured EU guarantees to scale sink investments toward 2040 neutrality.
- Pollution disclosure: material positive and negative impacts identified—reducing pollution via environmental financing and potential harms via financing high-pollution sectors; management via cross-cutting targets (SDG contribution, environment quota), sector sustainability guidelines, and exclusion lists, with detailed ESRS E2-1/E2-2/E2-3 information referenced elsewhere in the report.

- Climate change as a direct biodiversity driver is not separately required in the E&S Appraisal guidelines, aside from climate mainstreaming and the application of ESS6 in KfW Development Bank’s Sustainability Guideline; related impacts are managed through Paris-aligned sector guidelines and exclusion lists.
- Readers are referred to the general “Disclosures on ESG risks” for overarching ESG risk management targets, actions, and policies.
- On strategy resilience, KfW’s 2024 risk inventory evaluated biodiversity/ecosystem risk drivers—including ocean acidification, biodiversity-related resource scarcity, dependence on ecosystem services, land/sea use, pollution, animal welfare, species exploitation, and rising resource costs—and their influence across risk types.
- The principal transmission channel identified is via credit and equity investment risks if biodiversity loss increases counterparties’ probability of default. A two-step analysis screens sectors for biodiversity dependency/impact, then assesses at-risk partners’ ESG risk profiles after mitigation measures; stakeholders were not separately consulted.
- Outcome: No biodiversity risk drivers were classified as material in any risk type for financial year 2024.

nodes.title: Disclosures on climate and biodiversity risks
nodes.heading: 6.6 Disclosures on climate and biodiversity risks
nodes.start_phrase: For general information on KfW Group’s ESG risk management, including the existing targets, actions and policies in this regard, please refer to the “Disclosures on ESG risks” section in the “General information” chapter.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Environmental information within KfW Group’s Combined Non-Financial Report, focusing on biodiversity-related policies, risk disclosures, and strategic resilience.
- Policy framework: KfW applies IFC Performance Standards (or World Bank ESS for KfW Development Bank) within its E&S Appraisal, especially PS6/ESS6 (and ESS1 for ecosystem services).
- Biodiversity requirements under PS6/ESS6:
  - Identify and address threats such as habitat loss and fragmentation, invasive alien species, exploitation, hydrological changes, nutrient and other pollution.
  - Avoid impacts where possible; otherwise minimize and mitigate.
  - Exclude projects that would cause a net reduction in endangered or critically endangered species.
  - Prevent introduction of invasive species; prevent/mitigate land degradation; manage negative impacts on ecosystem extent, condition, and ecosystem services.
- Social safeguards: Through PS7/ESS7 (Indigenous Peoples), ensure informed and willing consent and appropriate consultation of local and Indigenous communities in financing activities.
- Scope limits: No additional KfW-specific policies on land use/agriculture, oceans/seas, or deforestation beyond those stated.
- Climate–biodiversity linkage: E&S Appraisal guidelines have no explicit climate requirements as a direct biodiversity driver, except climate mainstreaming and ESS6 within KfW Development Bank’s Sustainability Guideline; climate-related biodiversity impacts are managed via Paris-aligned sector guidelines and exclusion lists.
- Risk disclosures reference: Points readers to the general “Disclosures on ESG risks” section for broader ESG risk management targets, actions, and policies.
- Strategy resilience and risk assessment (FY 2024):
  - Assessed biodiversity/ecosystem risk drivers: ocean acidification, resource scarcity from biodiversity loss, dependence on ecosystem services, land and sea use, water/soil pollution, animal welfare, species exploitation, rising resource costs.
  - Primary transmission channels: credit and equity investment risks via increased probability of default of business partners.
  - Methodology: sector-based screening of counterparties’ biodiversity dependencies/impacts; for at-risk partners, ESG risk profile assessed (considering mitigation) to determine high-risk status in relevant biodiversity categories.
  - Stakeholder input: not separately included.
  - Outcome: no biodiversity risk drivers classified as material in any risk type for financial year 2024.

nodes.title: Resilience of KfW Group’s strategy and business model regarding biodiversity risks
nodes.heading: 6.6.1 Resilience of KfW Group’s strategy and business model regarding biodiversity risks
nodes.start_phrase:
KfW Group examined whether and to what extent ESG risk drivers impact KfW Group’s overall risk profile in 
the short term in the risk inventory of financial year 2024 (see “Risk management approach of KfW (overview)” 
in the “Risk report” chapter).
nodes.summary:
- Explains KfW Group’s biodiversity-related policy framework within its Environmental and Social (E&S) Appraisal, based on IFC Performance Standards or the World Bank Environmental and Social Standards (ESS), especially PS6/ESS6.
- Details PS6/ESS6 requirements: identify and manage biodiversity and ecosystem-service risks (e.g., habitat loss/fragmentation, invasive species, exploitation, hydrological changes, nutrient and other pollution); avoid or minimize impacts; prohibit projects causing net reductions in endangered species; prevent invasive species; mitigate impacts on ecosystems (including land degradation) and on ecosystem services.
- Addresses social aspects via PS7/ESS7 on Indigenous Peoples, ensuring informed and willing consent and necessary consultations.
- States KfW has no additional group-specific policies on land use/agriculture, oceans/seas, or deforestation beyond those standards.
- Notes climate change as a biodiversity driver is not directly required in E&S Appraisal guidelines except for climate mainstreaming and ESS6 in KfW Development Bank’s Sustainability Guideline; wider climate impacts are managed through Paris-aligned sector guidelines and exclusion lists.
- Points to separate “Disclosures on ESG risks” for broader climate and biodiversity risk information.
- Summarizes 2024 biodiversity risk analysis: identified drivers (ocean acidification, biodiversity-related resource scarcity, dependence on ecosystem services, land/sea use, pollution, animal welfare, species exploitation, rising resource costs); assessed impacts mainly via credit and equity risks through counterparties’ default probabilities using sector-based screening and ESG risk profiles; stakeholders not separately involved; outcome—no biodiversity risk drivers deemed material in 2024.
- Provides EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosure context: purpose of taxonomy, six environmental objectives, and the delegated acts/Commission Notices setting technical screening criteria.
- Clarifies reporting scope and timing: in 2024, financial institutions disclose taxonomy eligibility for all six objectives and alignment only for climate mitigation and adaptation; full alignment reporting across all six objectives begins in 2025.
- Specifies credit-institution KPIs and templates: Green Asset Ratio (GAR) per DDA Annex VI, nuclear/gas templates per Annex XII, qualitative disclosures per Annex XI; relies on counterparty-provided information; excludes banking operations from taxonomy reporting.
- Outlines regulatory scope: taxonomy applicability tied to European sustainability reporting; NFRD/CSR-RUG in force as of 31 Dec 2024 in Germany, with CSRD published but not yet transposed.

nodes.title: Disclosures in accordance with Article 8 of the EU Taxonomy
nodes.heading: 6.7 Disclosures in accordance with Article 8 of the EU Taxonomy
nodes.start_phrase: Substantial financial resources are required for the transformation to a sustainable economy.
nodes.summary:
- Section context: Environmental information within a combined non-financial report detailing disclosures required under Article 8 of the EU Taxonomy Regulation.
- Purpose and policy backdrop: Explains the EU’s sustainable finance agenda (2018 Action Plan; 2021 Strategy) aimed at redirecting capital toward environmentally sustainable activities through a standardized classification system (EU Taxonomy).
- EU Taxonomy scope: Defines environmentally sustainable (“taxonomy-aligned”) economic activities using technical screening criteria to increase transparency of capital flows.
- Environmental objectives covered: Six objectives—climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, sustainable use and protection of water and marine resources, transition to a circular economy, pollution prevention and control, and protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems.
- Regulatory and guidance framework: Details the delegated acts and notices establishing technical screening criteria and clarifications, including:
  - Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139 for mitigation and adaptation,
  - Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2485 expanding activities for those two objectives,
  - Complementary Climate Delegated Act (EU) 2022/1214 including nuclear and natural gas as transitional activities,
  - Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2486 for the other four objectives,
  - Related Commission notices addressing interpretation.
- Reporting obligations and phasing (Article 8/DDA): Vary by entity type and phase in over time.
  - 2024: Financial corporations report taxonomy eligibility for all six objectives and alignment only for mitigation and adaptation.
  - 2025: Full eligibility and alignment reporting for all six objectives.
- Credit institution disclosures: Must report taxonomy eligibility and alignment of financing activities, using counterparty information; disclose the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) per DDA Annex VI and nuclear/gas-related templates per Annex XII; provide qualitative disclosures per Annex XI; exclude banking operations processes from taxonomy reporting.
- Applicability in Germany: Reporting scope tied to European corporate sustainability reporting rules; at the 31 December 2024 reporting date, the NFRD (implemented via Germany’s CSR-RUG) remains in force, with CSRD adopted but not yet transposed.

nodes.title: Legal requirements in the context of the EU Taxonomy Regulation
nodes.heading: 6.7.1 Legal requirements in the context of the EU Taxonomy Regulation
nodes.start_phrase: Substantial financial resources are required for the transformation to a sustainable economy.
nodes.summary:
- Explains the EU Taxonomy Regulation’s purpose to redirect capital toward environmentally sustainable activities via a standardized classification system and technical screening criteria.
- Outlines the six environmental objectives under Article 9: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, water and marine resources, circular economy, pollution prevention and control, and biodiversity and ecosystems.
- Summarizes key delegated acts and guidance: 2021/2139 (criteria for mitigation/adaptation), 2023/2485 (additional activities), 2022/1214 (nuclear and gas transitional conditions), 2023/2486 (criteria for the other four objectives), and related Commission Notices.
- Details Article 8 disclosure obligations and phasing: in FY2024 financial institutions report eligibility for all six objectives and alignment for mitigation/adaptation only; full eligibility and alignment reporting across all six objectives begins in FY2025.
- Specifies credit institution reporting: the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) as the main KPI per DDA Annex VI, nuclear/fossil gas templates per Annex XII, qualitative disclosures per Annex XI, reliance on counterparty data, and exclusion of banking operations processes from taxonomy reporting.
- Clarifies the regulatory reporting scope linkage to European corporate sustainability reporting: NFRD (implemented in Germany via CSR-RUG) currently applicable; CSRD published in 2022 but not yet transposed in Germany by 31 December 2024.
- Describes KfW Group’s application: sustainability embedded in strategy; group-wide “tranSForm” project for sustainable finance; voluntary publication of taxonomy KPIs for FY2024; KfW IPEX-Bank has reported since FY2021 and is using consolidated reporting at the parent level for the first time.
- Notes limitations of taxonomy coverage for KfW’s portfolio: exclusions include sovereigns, supranationals, SMEs not subject to NFRD/CSRD, and non-EU counterparties—key segments for a public promotional bank—leading to low observed alignment rates due to scope, ambition level, and data gaps.
- States that taxonomy screening currently is not used to steer business sectors or individual financing decisions; product criteria in select programs reference taxonomy “substantial contribution” (e.g., Climate action campaign for corporates, Sustainable mobility for municipalities and companies, Green Transition Facility), but taxonomy is otherwise not central to product design.
- Sets out the reporting basis: assets measured at gross carrying amounts from IFRS consolidated financial statements; FinRep definitions used for counterparty type and product grouping; reporting at the regulatory consolidated group level consistent with the commercial consolidation; GAR defined as the share of taxonomy-aligned exposures in covered assets.

nodes.title: Application of the EU taxonomy within KfW Group
nodes.heading: 6.7.2 Application of the EU taxonomy within KfW Group
nodes.start_phrase: Sustainability in its actions is a particular priority and an overarching business objective for KfW Group.
nodes.summary:
- KfW Group positions sustainability as a core objective embedded in its mission, policies, and risk and business strategies.
- Through its tranSForm sustainable finance project, the group is implementing internal processes to meet EU Taxonomy reporting obligations.
- For the first time, KfW Group will voluntarily publish group-wide taxonomy KPIs under Article 8 of the EU Taxonomy Regulation for financial year 2024.
- KfW IPEX-Bank has reported mandatory EU taxonomy data since 2021 and, for 2024, is using consolidated reporting at the parent group level.
- The group supports a standardized taxonomy to enhance transparency and steer sustainable financing but stresses that KPIs must be meaningful and comparable.
- Large parts of KfW’s portfolio are excluded from mandatory taxonomy screening (e.g., financing to sovereigns and supranationals, SMEs not subject to NFRD/CSRD, and non-EU counterparties), which reflects its public promotional and international mandate.
- Current taxonomy scope centers on environmental/climate-relevant activities; many deserving sectors are not taxonomy-eligible, and data gaps plus stringent criteria lead to low alignment rates.
- Consequently, KfW has not used taxonomy screening to manage business lines or individual financing; product design has only selectively leveraged taxonomy criteria (notably “substantial contribution”) in specific programs and a VC fund (e.g., programme 293, programmes 267–269, Green Transition Facility).
- Taxonomy reporting basis: assets recognized at gross carrying amounts under IFRS consolidated financial statements, applying FinRep definitions for counterparty type and product grouping; scope aligns with the regulatory consolidated group, matching the commercial-law consolidation perimeter.
- The Green Asset Ratio (GAR) is defined as the share of taxonomy-aligned exposures within specified covered assets.

nodes.title: Basis for taxonomy reporting within KfW Group
nodes.heading: 6.7.3 Basis for taxonomy reporting within KfW Group
nodes.start_phrase: For taxonomy reporting, assets are recognised in gross carrying amounts on the basis of KfW Group’s consolidated financial statements prepared in accordance with the International Financial Reporting Standards (“IFRS”).
nodes.summary:
- Focus: How KfW Group applies the EU Taxonomy in its environmental reporting and builds taxonomy KPIs for the first time at group level for financial year 2024.
- Strategic stance: Sustainability is a core objective; KfW supports a standardized taxonomy to increase transparency but stresses KPIs must be meaningful and comparable.
- Voluntary reporting: Group-wide taxonomy KPIs disclosed under Article 8 for 2024; KfW IPEX-Bank has reported since 2021 and uses consolidated reporting at parent level for the first time.
- Limits of applicability: Large parts of KfW’s portfolio are outside mandatory taxonomy screening (e.g., sovereigns, central banks, supranationals, SMEs not under NFRD/CSRD, non-EU counterparties), and many sectors are not yet taxonomy-eligible.
- Data and alignment challenges: High ambition levels and limited data yield low alignment rates; taxonomy screening results are not yet used to manage business areas or individual financing decisions.
- Product design: Some programmes reflect taxonomy “substantial contribution” criteria (e.g., Climate action campaign for corporates, Sustainable mobility for municipalities and companies, Green Transition Facility), but the taxonomy otherwise has not steered product design to date.
- Reporting basis: Assets measured at gross carrying amounts per IFRS consolidated statements; FinRep definitions used for counterparty types and product groups; regulatory consolidated group matches the commercial consolidation scope.
- GAR and covered assets: GAR = share of taxonomy-aligned exposures in covered assets. Covered assets = total assets before risk provisions minus exposures to central governments, central banks, supranationals, and the trading portfolio. KfW has no trading assets; some derivatives appear in trading due to hedge accounting rules.
- Exclusions from eligibility: Transactions with non-NFRD/CSRD entities; derivatives (incl. hedge-accounted in templates), short-term interbank loans, cash and cash equivalents, and “other assets” (e.g., PPE, intangibles, tax assets, macro fair value hedge adjustments, and investments in subs/JVs/associates).
- Who is in scope: Exposures to NFRD/CSRD-obliged credit institutions, other financial corporations, and non-financial corporations are always eligible; households only if tied to residential mortgages, renovation, or motor vehicles; local/regional governments are in principle eligible but not assessed for 2024 due to lack of data.
- Determining NFRD/CSRD status: Based on Articles 19a/29a of Directive 2013/34/EU and the direct legal counterparty (EU-based, >500 employees, large undertaking, public interest, or has published mandatory taxonomy KPIs for FY2023). Published KPIs inform pro rata eligibility/alignment for transactions without known use of proceeds.
- Special treatments:
  - On-lending via financing partners is always included but reported as non-eligible/non-aligned in 2024 due to data gaps.
  - Local/regional government financing shown as non-eligible/non-aligned for 2024 due to no reporting obligations/data.
  - Environmentally sustainable bonds are included without checking NFRD/CSRD status.
- Known vs unknown use of proceeds:
  - Known use: Assess eligibility against listed economic activities; if eligible, test for alignment via three criteria—substantial contribution to one of six environmental objectives, do-no-significant-harm, and minimum social safeguards. If multiple attributable activities, classify as non-eligible/non-aligned.
  - Unknown use: Apply counterparties’ reported turnover and CapEx taxonomy KPIs pro rata; exclude blanket zero-result assessments.
- KPI inclusion: Exposures with known use that are eligible/aligned feed both turnover and CapEx KPIs; general corporate finance and most financial undertakings (except on-lending) rely on counterparties’ published KPIs for FY2023.
- Governance/process: A standardized, group-wide taxonomy assessment is applied; KfW IPEX-Bank has embedded taxonomy checks in its credit process and annually validates data for existing business since 2021.
- First-time disclosure caveat: No prior-year comparatives are presented for 2024.

nodes.title: Implementation of the taxonomy assessment process within KfW Group
nodes.heading: 6.7.4 Implementation of the taxonomy assessment process within KfW Group
nodes.start_phrase: The taxonomy criteria are checked on a case-by-case basis for every transaction based on the taxonomy reporting principles explained in the previous chapter.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: First-time EU Taxonomy reporting by KfW Group within the Combined Non-Financial Report (Environmental information) for the year ended 31 December 2024, covering eligibility and alignment for climate change mitigation and adaptation, and eligibility only for the other environmental objectives.

- Treatment of public-sector counterparties: Due to no reporting obligations and lack of data for financial year 2024 (confirmed by spot checks), transactions with local authorities and regional governments are not assessed and are reported as taxonomy-non-eligible/non-aligned under local governments financing.

- Counterparty and product coverage:
  - Non-financial corporations with a known use of proceeds: assessed for eligibility and, where applicable, for alignment.
  - Non-financial corporations without a known use of proceeds (general corporate financing) and financial undertakings (except on-lending): considered using the counterparties’ published taxonomy KPIs (turnover and CapEx) for FY 2023.
  - Exposures with several attributable economic activities are classified as taxonomy-non-eligible/non-aligned.
  - Transactions with limited informational value are excluded from the assessment.

- Assessment methodology:
  - Transaction-level eligibility check, then split into exposures with known vs unknown use of proceeds.
  - For known use: eligibility determined by link to a taxonomy-defined activity; alignment requires all three conditions—substantial contribution to one of six environmental objectives, do-no-significant-harm, and compliance with minimum social safeguards.
  - For unknown use: eligibility and alignment reported pro rata based on the business partner’s published taxonomy KPIs; blanket zero assessments are excluded.
  - Group-wide standardized rules apply, including to KfW IPEX-Bank, where taxonomy is embedded in the credit process; existing business is validated annually.
  - Other KfW Group sectors conduct an initial review of eligible existing business for FY 2024, supported by training and cross-sector engagement.

- Reporting process and integration:
  - For 2024, assessed transactions are aggregated centrally in Finance using FinRep data and included in Article 8 EU Taxonomy disclosures within the sustainability report approval process.
  - In 2025, processes will be fully integrated into BAU with expanded automation and enhanced data exchange with customers.

- Key 2024 disclosures (as of 31 December 2024):
  - Covered assets: EUR 460,085 million.
  - Exposures excluded from the numerator: 44.0% of covered assets, entirely due to counterparties not subject to NFRD/CSRD.
  - Eligibility and alignment overview: 56.0% of covered assets are eligible for taxonomy assessment; taxonomy‑eligible equals 2.3% of turnover and CapEx; taxonomy‑aligned (GAR) equals 0.2% of turnover and CapEx.
  - No prior-year comparatives, as this is first-time reporting.
  - Business sector contributions differ due to sector-specific characteristics.

nodes.title: Disclosures by KfW Group on the EU taxonomy as of 31 December 2024
nodes.heading: 6.7.5 Disclosures by KfW Group on the EU taxonomy as of 31 December 2024
nodes.start_phrase: As of the reporting date of 31 December 2024, KfW Group is reporting for the first time on the proportion of its taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned economic activities for the environmental objectives of climate change mitigation and climate change adaptation.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and rollout: KfW Group is implementing EU Taxonomy (Article 8) disclosures, with 2024 as the first reporting year for taxonomy-eligible and -aligned activities for climate change mitigation and adaptation. Data are aggregated from FinRep, quality-assured, consolidated by Finance, and integrated into sustainability report approval processes. Full integration into standard operating processes and expanded automation/data exchange is planned for 2025, supported by extensive cross-sector engagement, training, and dialogue.

- Scope and key 2024 metrics:
  - Covered assets: EUR 460,085 million.
  - 44% of covered assets are excluded from the GAR numerator, entirely due to counterparties not subject to NFRD/CSRD.
  - 56% of covered assets are eligible for taxonomy assessment.
  - Taxonomy-eligible business: 2.3% (turnover KPI and CapEx KPI).
  - Taxonomy-aligned (GAR): 0.2% (turnover KPI and CapEx KPI).
  - For non-climate environmental objectives, only taxonomy eligibility is reported (as required).

- Sector-specific coverage and data gaps:
  - SME Bank & Private Clients and Customised Finance & Public Clients: On-lending via financing partners (51% of covered assets) and municipal financing cannot be assessed in 2024 due to insufficient data; reporting focuses on refinancing of financial undertakings outside on-lending and select loans to non-financial undertakings. A future assessment approach for on-lending is being coordinated with the German banking industry.
  - Financial Markets: Assessment covers bonds in the liquidity portfolio and executed money market transactions.
  - Export and project finance (KfW IPEX-Bank): Large portions are out of scope because many counterparties are outside the EU or not subject to NFRD/CSRD (including SPEs), even when financing purposes relate to EU taxonomy-eligible activities.
  - KfW Development Bank and DEG: Financing outside the EU is not eligible for taxonomy assessment due to counterparties not being subject to NFRD/CSRD.
  - KfW Capital: Fund investments are not eligible as funds are not subject to NFRD/CSRD.
  - Retail exposure is limited to education financing and employee loans (non-real-estate/vehicle).

- Resulting coverage constraints: A significant share (44%) of the portfolio is out of scope, and much of the in-scope portion lacks sufficient data for eligibility assessment, leading to low taxonomy-eligible (2.3%) and -aligned (0.2% GAR) shares.

- Nuclear and fossil gas activities: Following the Complementary Climate Delegated Act (EU) 2022/1214, related exposures are restricted by KfW policies but may appear via counterparties’ general KPIs; in 2024, included items have no known use-of-proceeds allocations to such activities.

- Comparison with KfW’s environment quota: In 2024, 44% of new financing contributed to KfW’s environment quota, which is not comparable to the GAR due to different bases (new commitments vs. existing business), scope exclusions, and stringent GAR documentation/verification requirements. GAR is not currently used as a management KPI.

- Reporting templates and methodology notes: Taxonomy KPI templates for credit institutions (Annex VI DDA) and for nuclear/gas (Annex XII DDA) are published separately, with rounding conventions and sector breakdowns based on the direct legal counterparty’s main activity. Proportion calculations align covered assets with the GAR denominator and taxonomy-aligned exposures with the GAR numerator.

nodes.title: Additional information on the tables in the appendix
nodes.heading: 6.7.6 Additional information on the tables in the appendix
nodes.start_phrase:
The taxonomy templates for the taxonomy KPIs of credit institutions of Annex VI DDA to be reported 
pursuant to Article 4 DDA are published in the “Taxonomy tables pursuant to Annex VI/XII (EU) 2021/2178 (DDA)” chapter.
nodes.summary:
- Explains EU Taxonomy developments: the Complementary Climate Delegated Act (EU) 2022/1214 adds nuclear and fossil gas activities; KfW heavily restricts such financing but taxonomy-eligible/aligned exposures can include counterparties’ reported nuclear/gas activities when use of proceeds is unknown.
- Describes KfW’s environment quota metric (used since 2012): in 2024, 44% of financing contributed. Clarifies major differences from the EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR): environment quota is based on annual new commitments, GAR on existing business; large lending segments are excluded from the GAR numerator and stringent documentation/verification means few transactions qualify. GAR is not used for group steering.
- Provides guidance on taxonomy reporting templates: publication location (Annex VI/XII DDA), rounding rules, separate turnover and CapEx templates, sector breakdown by main activity of the direct business partner. Nuclear/gas templates apply only to NFRD/CSRD-subject counterparties; for proportions, “covered assets” map to the GAR denominator and “taxonomy-aligned exposures” to the GAR numerator.
- Introduces the Social information chapter in the context of KfW’s Strategic objectives 2029 and the secondary objective “employee potential and customer centricity,” targeting employer attractiveness, customer satisfaction, brand awareness/profiling, and diversity.
- Outlines the chapter’s four sections: (1) Social matters at KfW Group (foundational guidelines, human rights policy linked to the Code of Conduct); (2) Social matters in banking operations (diversity, remuneration, working conditions, participation; “Employer positioning” project); (3) Social matters in the banking business (impacts on value chain workers, communities, customers, and corporate customers); (4) Complaints management and channels for employees, customers, affected parties, and other stakeholders.
- Lists human rights and sustainability standards KfW commits to or considers: UN human rights instruments (UDHR, Covenants, CRPD), ECHR, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, ILO Core Labour Standards, OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises, IFC Performance Standards, Equator Principles, European DFIs’ human rights principles/policies, and the Diversity Charter.

structure.title: Social information
structure.heading: 7 Social information
structure.start_phrase:
The fulfilment of KfW’s “sustainable promotion” purpose is operationalised in the strategic objectives 2029, 
as described in the “Strategic objectives 2029” section in the “Basic information on KfW Group” chapter of the financial report, including in the context of secondary objectives.
structure.summary:
- Overview of the “Social information” chapter within KfW’s combined non-financial report, linked to the Group’s “sustainable promotion” purpose and Strategic Objectives 2029.
- Emphasis on the secondary objective “employee potential and customer centricity,” highlighting workforce and customers as key success factors for sustainable business, with goals for employer attractiveness, customer satisfaction, brand awareness, brand profiling, and diversity.
- Chapter structure:
  1) Social matters at KfW Group: foundations of social responsibility, human rights policy, and Code of Conduct setting ethical standards for employees and external partners.
  2) Social matters in banking operations: diversity, remuneration, working conditions, and worker participation, focusing on employee satisfaction, non-discriminatory pay, work-life balance, gender equality, and inclusion; measures consolidated under the group-wide “Employer positioning” strategic project; commitment to compliance, fairness, and employer attractiveness.
  3) Social matters in the banking business: impacts and opportunities of KfW’s business for value chain workers, affected communities, and customers, including a KfW-specific impact on corporate customers.

- Strategic importance reflected through identified material impacts and opportunities discussed in the chapter.
