nodes.title: Social matters at KfW Group
nodes.heading: 7.1 Social matters at KfW Group
nodes.start_phrase: KfW Group commits to the following agreements and declarations in its human rights policy (“Policy statement of KfW and its subsidiaries on human rights and on its human rights strategy”) and the Code of Conduct:
nodes.summary:
- Strategic framing: Social information is tied to KfW’s Strategic Objectives 2029, especially the secondary objective “employee potential and customer centricity,” targeting employer attractiveness, customer satisfaction, brand awareness/profiling, and diversity.
- Chapter structure:
  1) Social matters at KfW Group (foundations, policies, human rights, Code of Conduct)
  2) Social matters in banking operations (workforce: diversity, remuneration, working conditions, participation)
  3) Social matters in the banking business (impacts on value-chain workers, affected communities, customers; corporate customer impacts)
  4) Complaints management (channels and handling for employees, customers, affected parties, stakeholders)
- Human rights policy and commitments: Alignment with UN instruments (UDHR, Covenants, CRPD, UNGPs), ILO Core Labour Standards, OECD Guidelines, IFC Performance Standards, Equator Principles, EDFI principles, and the Diversity Charter; group-wide applicability, Executive Board accountability, and stakeholder dialogue.
- LkSG implementation: Annual/ad hoc human rights and environmental risk analyses, risk-based prioritization, preventive and remedial actions, updates triggered by business changes or complaints; lower relevance of certain risks due to German-based workforce.
- Labour rights and safeguards: Commitment to ban child/forced labour and trafficking; uphold freedom of association, collective bargaining, non-discriminatory pay, equal opportunity (gender, origin, ethnicity, religion, political beliefs, disability, age, sexual identity), and rights to recreation, health, and safety; immediate action on violations; risk-based controls.
- Integration into business processes: Use of group-wide exclusion list and sustainability guidelines (Environmental and Social Appraisal Guidelines) to embed human rights and environmental considerations.
- Resources: Allocation of financial and human resources to manage material social impacts.
- Code of Conduct: Group-wide rules for leadership and employees, also guiding external partners; covers risk culture, diversity and inclusion, non-discrimination, leadership culture, skills development, data protection; commits to OECD/FATF principles; annually reviewed with possible ad hoc updates; individual accountability for compliance.
- Banking operations focus and materiality: Positive workforce impacts identified; “Employer positioning” project anchors measures across diversity, leadership, development, remuneration, working conditions to enhance employer attractiveness.
- Employer positioning project: 2023–2030, applies to all employees in Germany; seven dimensions—purpose-driven company (including ESG, diversity, inclusion), leadership, collaboration, flexibility (time/place), conditions (remuneration), development, and infrastructure; co-created with employees and representative bodies; ongoing communication via newsletters and info events.
- Diversity and inclusion: Group-wide commitment to equal opportunities and inclusive communication; KfW, KfW IPEX-Bank, KfW Capital signatories of the Diversity Charter; ambitions embedded in Equal Opportunities Plans and Inclusion Agreement and reflected in remuneration strategies; employee appreciation central to sustainability mission statement.
- Governance nuances and legal bases: Different legal forms lead to company-specific policies and targets; group-wide commitment to gender equality, including pay, anchored in Strategic Objectives 2029 and Equal Opportunities Plans in line with the German Federal Equality Act (BGleiG).
- Complaints and transparency: Structured mechanisms for receiving and addressing concerns from employees, customers, affected communities, and other stakeholders to support compliance and an open corporate culture.

nodes.title: Social matters in banking operations
nodes.heading: 7.2 Social matters in banking operations
nodes.start_phrase:
Social matters in banking operations relate to the group’s own workforce, which comprises both KfW Group 
employees and non-employees, and include issues related to equal treatment/non-discrimination and corporate culture alongside general working conditions.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on social matters in banking operations, covering both employees and non-employees and addressing equal treatment, non-discrimination, corporate culture, and working conditions.
- Materiality assessment identified positive impacts for KfW Group’s workforce; aligned with the strategic objectives 2029 via the secondary objective “Employee potential/customer centricity.”
- Introduction of the “Employer positioning” project (launched 2023, running to 2030) to enhance employer attractiveness, customer satisfaction, brand awareness, brand profiling, and diversity; applies to all KfW Group employees in Germany.
- Strategic employer positioning built on seven dimensions: company with purpose (incl. ESG, diversity and inclusion), leadership, collaboration, flexibility (work hours/place), conditions (remuneration), further development, and infrastructure.
- Implementation anchored in group business sector planning with allocated resources; strong employee and works council involvement through surveys and workshops; regular internal communications via quarterly newsletters and semiannual info events.
- Diversity and inclusion framed by the human rights policy and Code of Conduct; KfW, KfW IPEX-Bank, and KfW Capital are signatories of the Diversity Charter.
- Ambitions and actions for diversity and inclusion embedded in Equal Opportunities Plans and the Inclusion Agreement; also reflected in remuneration strategies.
- Sustainability mission underscores employee appreciation and highlights qualified, motivated staff as a key success factor.
- Recognition of differing legal bases across KfW and subsidiaries, resulting in company-specific policies and targets.
- Firm commitment to gender equality, including pay equity, included in strategic objectives 2029 and anchored in KfW and DEG Equal Opportunities Plans pursuant to the German Federal Equality Act (BGleiG).

nodes.title: Diversity and inclusion
nodes.heading: 7.2.1 Diversity and inclusion
nodes.start_phrase: KfW Group strives to provide equal and fair opportunities and communication channels to all individuals irrespective of any linguistic, cultural or other differences.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and materiality: Social matters in banking operations focus on KfW Group’s own workforce (employees and non-employees), covering equal treatment/non-discrimination, corporate culture and working conditions. A materiality assessment found positive impacts for the workforce, anchoring the secondary objective “Employee potential/customer centricity” in Strategy 2029.

- Employer positioning project (2023–2030): Strategic framework to enhance employer attractiveness across seven dimensions (purpose incl. D&I, leadership, collaboration, flexibility, conditions/remuneration, development, infrastructure). Co-developed with employee/manager input via surveys and workshops; ongoing communication through newsletters and information events.

- Diversity and inclusion policy framework: Group-wide commitment via human rights policy and Code of Conduct; KfW, KfW IPEX-Bank, and KfW Capital signed the Diversity Charter. Gender equality (including pay) is embedded in Strategy 2029 and formalised in Equal Opportunities Plans (KfW and DEG) and an Inclusion Agreement.

- Equal Opportunities governance:
  - KfW: Sixth Equal Opportunities Plan effective 1 Jan 2024–31 Dec 2027; midterm evaluation after two years; implementation by managers with HR support; transparency via intranet/website.
  - DEG: Plan effective 1 Jan 2023–31 Dec 2027; objectives in gender empowerment, work-life blend, gender pay, and gender balance; monitored by Management and Supervisory Boards.

- Key D&I actions:
  - Group-wide gender-appropriate language policy.
  - KfW (by end-2027): expand women’s career advancement communications; introduce bias awareness training; ensure equitable promotion/development (incl. focus on women with severe disabilities); uphold pay equity; analyze careers post family-care measures; set target salaries for transfers/promotions; support “second-life careers” for parents; increase women in non-tariff roles and STEM via role models, networking and targeted outreach; promote part-time leadership/job shares; maintain balanced talent pools; mentoring/shadowing/group coaching; ensure gender-balanced hiring processes with female manager involvement; set reference values for senior specialist roles.
  - Inclusion for people with disabilities (KfW): Inclusion Agreement (2015) with seven target areas; recruitment access measures; myAbility talent programme; accessible workplaces and tools; additional benefits; sign-language support; awareness workshops and inclusion days; managerial support incl. external consulting; ongoing without end date.
  - KfW IPEX-Bank: Targets for women in leadership per German law; “Leadership Prospects” programme (needs analysis, workshops, coaching, mentoring, shadowing); “Female Leaders of IPEX” network; targeted recruiting days and outreach to female candidates; ongoing continuation of proven formats.
  - DEG: Targeted support for high-potential women (mentoring, training); surveys to reduce barriers to leadership; encourage board mandates/project leadership; develop a job-share marketplace; ensure proportional promotions.

- Targets and KPIs:
  - KfW target for employees with severe disabilities: 6% (above statutory 5%); status reviewed semi-annually.
  - Group D&I KPI: External Diversity Index (Fki Diversity for Success) target 85/100 by 2029; current 80 (2023); measured annually 2023–2029.
  - KfW Equal Opportunities Plan: embed equal opportunities in culture, remove structural disadvantages, improve work–family/care reconciliation, and raise women’s share in management/senior specialist roles; impact indicators include number of job shares and part-time leadership.
  - KfW IPEX-Bank: gender quotas for all management levels and Supervisory Board, measured quarterly to a 30 June 2027 target date; annual 60% female graduate trainee quota (2024 target not met due to applicant pool; actual reported share 48.3% vs. 60% target).
  - DEG: targets for women’s share in potential pool (two selection stages) and development programmes; gender balance across management levels, based on legal requirements and feasibility modelling.

- Reported workforce metrics (31 Dec 2024, headcount basis):
  - Total employees: 8,838 (Germany 8,387; rest of world 451).
  - Gender: 4,261 female; 4,577 male.
  - Contracts: 7,827 permanent; 1,011 temporary.
  - Top management (level below Executive Board): 29.7% female (11 of 37).
  - Age distribution: <30: 1,133; 30–50: 4,664; >50: 3,041.
  - Turnover: 5.3% (454 departures), excluding temporary expiries/internal moves/secondments.

- Remuneration policies and oversight:
  - Group-wide remuneration strategy per Section 27 InstitutsVergV: transparent, non-discriminatory systems for employees with German contracts; local-law remuneration abroad guided by employment guidelines.
  - Objectives: align with business/risk strategy; support attraction/retention; transparency across roles/companies; standardised performance management; avoid risk-prone incentives; regulatory compliance.
  - Governance: KfW oversees subsidiary compliance; annual reviews of risks/misguided incentives, guarantees, severance, retention awards, bonus caps, total variable pay, hedging; KfW must be involved in any new/revised systems; supervisory bodies monitor appropriateness and set total variable pay; subsidiaries perform annual adequacy reviews and report; KfW Executive Board accountable for system appropriateness and supervisory reporting.

nodes.title: Remuneration
nodes.heading: 7.2.2 Remuneration
nodes.start_phrase: The group-wide remuneration strategy policy in accordance with Section 27 of the Remuneration Regulation for Institutions (Institutsvergütungsverordnung – “InstitutsVergV”) sets out the overall parameters for remuneration within KfW Group.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and governance: Group-wide remuneration strategy under Section 27 InstitutsVergV sets transparent, non-discriminatory pay principles and performance management for all KfW Group employees with German contracts; foreign local hires follow employment guidelines aligned with regulatory requirements. KfW, as parent, annually reviews subsidiaries’ compliance (e.g., risk alignment, variable pay caps, severance, retention awards, hedging) and must be involved in any new or revised remuneration systems. Supervisory bodies monitor appropriateness and set total variable pay.

- Objectives of remuneration strategy: align pay with business and risk strategy; support attraction/retention; ensure transparency for role changes; standardize performance and pay processes; avoid excessive risk incentives; ensure clarity and regulatory compliance.

- Subsidiary frameworks: KfW IPEX-Bank, DEG, and KfW Capital have subordinate strategies/bylaws detailing roles and metrics; annual appropriateness checks vs business/risk strategies; documented results go to supervisory bodies; KfW’s Executive Board oversees remuneration structure and reports annually.

- Collective bargaining and employment terms: In Germany, employees covered by the public banks’ collective agreement receive defined terms for pay, hours, leave, and termination; non-covered employees have comparable conditions via staff/works agreements. KfW Capital is not bound by collective bargaining.

- Oversight committees and transparency: Remuneration committees at KfW, DEG, KfW IPEX-Bank, and KfW Capital support supervisory oversight of employee and managing director remuneration, including annual reviews of metrics, variable pay pools, performance/retention periods, and regulatory compliance (InstitutsVergV; WpIVergV/WpIG for KfW Capital). Implementation of Germany’s pay transparency law enables employees to request gender-neutral pay information; KfW Capital applies case-by-case due to headcount.

- Actions to ensure fair and gender-neutral pay: Use of grading/salary bands to anchor equal pay; proactive identification of “structural cases” (notably women and part-time staff) before salary reviews to guide targeted, sustainable adjustments; continuous monitoring of departmental gender pay gaps during reviews; positive impacts observed for non-pay-scale levels. DEG is enhancing analytics (gender, age, tenure, function), using external benchmarks, requiring justification where equalization is not granted, and balancing performance, incentives, and structural equality.

- External certification: 2024 independent pay equity analyses by Lurse AG for KfW, KfW IPEX-Bank, and DEG resulted in pay equity certificates (valid two years); FPI Universal Fair Pay Analyst status awarded (valid one year). Reassessments and potential recertifications planned for 2025.

- Benefits and conditions: Employer-financed pensions (including disability and survivor benefits) for German contracts; additional options include deferred pension savings, mobility benefits (commuting cost reimbursement, Deutschlandticket, parking), private accident insurance; at KfW and DEG also low-interest building loans, occupational incapacity insurance, capital accumulation benefits, and from 2024 bicycle leasing (also at KfW Capital).

- Targets and effectiveness: Qualitative objectives focus on non-discriminatory, transparent pay; KfW’s Equal Opportunities Plan emphasizes identifying/removing structural disadvantages; effectiveness tracked via salary trends for new hires/transfers. DEG targets greater data transparency, gender-sensitive policy, and avoiding structural discrimination, with measurement starting 2024.

- Metrics (2024): 25.7% collective bargaining coverage in the EEA; 98.8% of EEA employees have workplace representation. All employees received adequate wages based on minimum wage checks (EEA) and multi-criteria reviews (non-EEA). Unadjusted ESRS gender pay gap is 14.0% (average gross hourly pay basis, accrual accounting, includes fixed/variable and in-kind benefits). Pay ratio of highest-paid individual to median employee is 10.6; median is lowered by 28.1% part-time share and inclusion of interns/trainees. Metrics are as of 31 December 2024.

- Working conditions policies: Emphasis on flexible working hours and work-life balance to support employability and performance; policies derive from mandate and business strategy and are codified in procedural rules agreed with Staff/Works Councils for German contracts, adhering to occupational safety and workplace regulations (Arbeitsschutzgesetz, Arbeitsstättenverordnung) and broader social policy commitments.

nodes.title: Working conditions
nodes.heading: 7.2.3 Working conditions
nodes.start_phrase: For KfW Group, for example, the structure of working hours and the promotion of work-life balance are key aspects when it comes to fulfilling employees’ individual needs and supporting their performance.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Social information section covering collective bargaining coverage, social dialogue, remuneration and pay equity, working conditions, actions and targets, and workforce engagement procedures.

- Collective bargaining and workplace representation:
  - Presents coverage rates for EEA countries with >50 employees that account for >10% of headcount.
  - Shows range categories (0–19% to 80–100%) for both collective bargaining coverage and workplace representation, highlighting Germany.
  
- Remuneration and pay equity:
  - 2024 adequacy review found all KfW Group employees received an adequate wage; EEA focus on statutory minimum wage; non-EEA adequacy determined via multiple criteria.
  - Unadjusted ESRS gender pay gap: 14.0% (methodology and included pay components detailed; accrual basis).
  - Pay ratio (highest-paid to median employee): 10.6; note that 28.1% part-time and inclusion of interns, student workers, and trainees lower the median. Metrics on accrual basis as of 31 Dec 2024.

- Working conditions policies and legal framework:
  - Policies derived from mandate and strategy, aimed at employability, sustainable work environment, and employer attractiveness.
  - German employees governed by procedural rules agreed with Staff/Works Councils; compliance with German OSH and labor laws (e.g., Arbeitsschutzgesetz, Arbeitsstättenverordnung, SGB VII, Mutterschutzgesetz, BetrVG).
  - Foreign contracts follow local labor/health protection law; assignments abroad may apply German labor/social security as relevant.

- Key aspects and OSH management:
  - Emphasis on flexible hours/locations and balancing work, family, caregiving, and personal life.
  - Agreements on mobile working, workations, and working hours (KfW and subsidiaries).
  - Preventative occupational health and safety management, ergonomic workplaces, decentralised risk assessments, focus on non-office roles and vulnerable individuals.

- Actions to implement policies:
  - Flexible work models: various part-time options, flexitime, and mobile working (60:40 remote/office at KfW, KfW IPEX-Bank, DEG; no fixed ratio at KfW Capital).
  - Additional leave and sabbaticals to support work-life balance; new option since July 2024 for up to 20 working days of mobile working abroad per year (pro rata), with DEG planning alignment.
  - Family and caregiving support: parent–child offices; onsite daycare in Frankfurt; reserved childcare places; access to external family services (emergency/virtual childcare, databases, holiday programs, event childcare, babysitter/au pair assistance). DEG offers childcare allowance, emergency care, 15 reintegration childcare places, holiday program, and a parents’ academy.
  - Networks and programs: KfW fathers’ network and membership in Conpadres; caregiving program with care guides, consultations, 24/7 hotline.
  - Support across life stages: option to work beyond statutory retirement age; reverse mentoring; expansion of management job sharing (including cross‑age pairing) under planning.
  - DEG Equal Opportunities Plan actions to enhance flexible work, reduce obstacles (including for fathers taking parental leave), and maintain “audit workandfamily” certification.

- International workforce:
  - Local staff in foreign offices receive working conditions and benefits at or above local legal standards, benchmarked to comparable international employers; efforts to apply German policies where suitable; additional benefits for international assignments reflecting local conditions and safety/economic factors.

- Targets and effectiveness:
  - Group-level focus on enabling mobile working and a results-based culture; no overarching quantitative targets; effectiveness tracked via employee surveys, turnover, and application trends.
  - KfW monitors qualitative outcomes under its Equal Opportunities Plan (e.g., childcare capacity and usage, caregiving services).
  - Employer attractiveness KPI for Strategy 2029: internal (engagement index from employee survey) and external (market research index on visibility/intention to apply) with peer benchmarking; survey limitations mitigated by qualitative follow-ups.
  - DEG targets to expand part-time and job-sharing in management, create additional capacity for job-share roles, and establish a job‑share marketplace; aims to increase uptake of flexible models and parental leave by men; maintain Hertie Foundation certification.

- Workforce engagement and representation procedures:
  - Due to differing legal regimes (BpersVG, BetrVG), no group-wide works council; each company uses its own procedures.
  - No legal requirement for a European works council (EWC/SE/SCE) arrangement.

nodes.title: Procedures for engaging with the own workforce and workers’ representatives
nodes.heading: 7.2.4 Procedures for engaging with the own workforce and workers’ representatives
nodes.start_phrase: Due to the various laws on employee participation (German Federal Personnel Representation Act [Bundespersonalvertretungsgesetz – “BpersVG”] and the German Works Constitution Act) it is not possible to create a works council for KfW Group as a whole.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on employer positioning and measurement: Introduction of an “Employer attractiveness” KPI tied to strategic objectives 2029, combining internal and external components. Internal attractiveness is tracked via a validated, benchmarkable engagement index from the regular employee survey; limitations are mitigated through qualitative follow-ups. External attractiveness is a weighted index (e.g., visibility, intention to apply) benchmarked biennially by an external research institute.

- DEG work-life blend initiatives and targets: Plans to add at least 0.2 FTE capacity when filling management job-share roles and to launch a job-share marketplace. Ongoing “audit workandfamily” certification supports work-life balance. Aim to increase male uptake of part-time/parental leave and expand flexible, part-time, and job-sharing options in management. Targets by 2027: part-time management (incl. job-share partner) 8 (2024 actual: 8); management job shares 4 (2024 actual: 3). Targets currently defined only for DEG.

- Workforce representation and engagement framework: Due to legal structure, no group-wide works council; each entity has tailored arrangements. KfW operates under the Federal Personnel Representation Act with General and Local Staff Councils; KfW IPEX-Bank and DEG have works councils and supervisory boards with elected worker representatives under the Works Constitution Act; KfW Capital has no works council due to size but uses informal dialogue formats. Additional bodies include equal opportunities officers, youth/trainee representatives, and representatives for severely disabled employees.

- Structured dialogue and inclusion processes: Regular, scheduled exchanges between HR leadership and representative bodies (monthly/fortnightly/six-weekly). Early and broad involvement in change processes via briefings, events, and intranet. Team charters support collaboration; grievance channels are available group-wide. Foreign sites engage employees directly.

- Employee surveys and continuous improvement: Group-wide, external, biennial survey since 2014 with stakeholder co-design, enabling time-series comparison and open comments. Results drive follow-up at all organizational levels with transparent communication; analysis respects minimum participant thresholds. The 2023 survey focused on KfWplus agenda, employer attractiveness, and culture; DEG conducts parallel in-depth analysis. Targeted surveys (2024) on childcare and caregiving inform work-life balance actions.

- Remuneration governance stakeholder inclusion: Shareholders involved via supervisory bodies and remuneration committees; employees influence remuneration-related agreements through staff/works councils. Supervisory boards at KfW IPEX-Bank and DEG include one-third worker representatives, with worker participation in remuneration committees. DEG ensures transparency through published remuneration reports and rights under the Transparency of Remuneration Act.

- Social matters in banking operations and value chain: Emphasis on downstream value chain workers (employees of financed firms, on-lending partners, funds, and trading partners) and affected communities, including indigenous peoples. Influence over some actors is limited; reliance on legal compliance and, in higher-risk developing contexts, on counterpart environmental and social management systems. The Code of Conduct guides externals and partners.

- Environmental and Social (E&S) due diligence: Group-wide E&S Appraisal applies to domestic promotional business, project/export finance, and development projects, anchored in business-sector sustainability guidelines. Domestic promotional business integrates a human rights policy aiming to avoid involvement in human rights violations. KfW Development Bank aligns with World Bank ESS2, WBG EHS Guidelines, and ILO Core Labour Standards; implementation/monitoring consultants oversee on-site compliance and corrective actions.

nodes.title: Social matters in the banking business
nodes.heading: 7.3 Social matters in the banking business
nodes.start_phrase: The fact that the business sectors specialise in various financing and promotional products translates into different impacts, risks and opportunities in KfW Group’s banking business with regard to social issues.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on social matters within KfW Group’s banking business, highlighting impacts, risks, and opportunities across different business sectors and their value chains.
- Identification of key stakeholders: value chain workers, affected communities, consumers/end-users, and corporate customers.
- Emphasis on downstream value chain workers (employees of financed companies, financing partners, funds/business partners), with limited influence over on-lending banks and other intermediaries and limited data availability.
- Reliance on applicable laws/regulations for value chain entities; in developing and emerging markets, expectation of effective environmental and social (E&S) management systems due to higher risk and weaker government controls.
- Code of Conduct serves as guidance for external partners and institutions.
- Affected communities addressed, including recognition of indigenous peoples as particularly vulnerable.
- Group-wide requirement for E&S Appraisals across domestic promotional business, project/export finance, and projects in developing/emerging countries; procedures anchored in sector-specific sustainability guidelines.
- Domestic promotional business guideline commits to respect and protect human rights and to avoid involvement in human rights violations; applies E&S standards referenced in the Environmental information chapter.
- KfW Development Bank applies World Bank ESS2 (Labor and Working Conditions), World Bank Group EHS Guidelines, and ILO Core Labour Standards; project consultants monitor on-site compliance (occupational safety, working conditions, resident protection) and address shortcomings.

nodes.title: Value chain workers and affected communities
nodes.heading: 7.3.1 Value chain workers and affected communities
nodes.start_phrase: Downstream value chain workers of KfW Group include employees of financed companies in direct business, employees of financing partners in the on-lending business and employees of funds and business partners in liquidity management (e.g. issuers of debt securities and trading partners).
nodes.summary:
- Scope and stakeholders: Outlines KfW Group’s approach to social matters across its banking value chain, focusing on downstream value chain workers, affected communities, consumers/end-users, and corporate customers.

- Group-wide policies and standards: Applies Environmental & Social (E&S) Appraisal to all relevant financing; aligns with World Bank ESS (notably ESS2, ESS5, ESS7), IFC Performance Standards, ILO Core Labour Standards, Equator Principles, Modern Slavery Act, and KfW’s human rights policy and Code of Conduct; uses exclusion lists and a “do no harm” and mitigation hierarchy approach; requires FPIC where indigenous peoples are affected; establishes grievance/complaints mechanisms and incident reporting.

- Business sector specifics:
  - Domestic promotional business: Human rights integrated into E&S Appraisal; aims to exclude human rights violations.
  - KfW Development Bank: Applies WB standards and ILO; uses consultants to monitor labor and community protections; can conduct Human Rights Impact Assessments; prepares Indigenous Peoples Plans and resettlement/livelihood restoration plans per ESS5; enforces incident reporting; maintains an expert network and mandatory E&S training; runs FALKE initiative to strengthen human-rights due diligence by 2026.
  - KfW IPEX-Bank: Assesses human rights, labor, OHS, and community risks; addresses trafficking/forced/child labor; requires compliance with IFC PS7 on indigenous peoples.
  - DEG: Applies IFC PS, exclusion lists, and E&S action plans; annual monitoring; can mandate external oversight; offers support beyond compliance; measures development impact via DERa 2.0 with a portfolio target of 32 points (achieved ~35 in 2024); supports gender outcomes via 2X Challenge; builds internal E&S capacity and training.
  - KfW Capital: Requires funds to have ESG policies, exclusion and grievance mechanisms, and to respect human rights/ILO standards; excludes investments impacting indigenous land without documented consent; sets minimum ESG criteria and checks whistleblowing/compliance systems.

- Engagement processes: Early stakeholder engagement through grievance mechanisms and structured dialogues; targeted analyses (e.g., gender, stakeholder) to identify risks/opportunities; DEG reviewed under the Operating Principles for Impact Management.

- Actions and controls: Job creation/retention through financing; environmental/biodiversity projects improving community living conditions; stronger safeguards in developing/emerging markets; contractual enforcement including payment stops or termination if E&S requirements not met; monitoring and annual reporting obligations.

- 2024 cases and performance: Three potential social/human-rights conflict cases (Indonesia, Tanzania, China/Xinjiang) under review with remediation steps initiated; no confirmed non-respect of UNGPs/ILO/OECD guidelines or severe human-rights incidents involving value chain workers; none reported for consumers/end-users.

- Targets and impact tracking: Sustainability mission requires consideration of social risks/impacts; SDG mapping used to track contributions, notably SDG 8 (decent work), SDG 9 (infrastructure/innovation), and SDG 11 (sustainable cities/communities); development of job-related impact indicators under group impact management; KfW Development Bank evaluates project effectiveness, publishes results in a transparency portal (84% of 2021/22 projects rated successful).

- Consumers and end-users (KfW only): Ensures non-discriminatory access to financing (energy-efficient housing, home ownership, education/student loans); governed by KfW Law, bylaws, and ministry mandates; covered by domestic sustainability guideline and human rights policy; no incidents or violations reported in 2024.

nodes.title: Customers – Consumers and end-users
nodes.heading: 7.3.2 Customers – Consumers and end-users
nodes.start_phrase: In the sense of the value chain described in the “KfW Group’s value chain” section in the “General information” chapter, private individuals are customers who either receive financing directly from KfW, such as student loan recipients, or who take out real estate loans, for instance, through the on-lending business.
nodes.summary:
- DERa 2.0 development effectiveness framework: two pillars (customer impact and DEG-supported transformation), five impact categories (decent jobs, local income, market/sector development, environmental stewardship, community effects), mix of quantitative/qualitative indicators (incl. World Bank data), net impact scoring (can be negative), project life-cycle application with baseline and five‑year ex‑ante estimates, annual updates, and portfolio management/reporting. Target portfolio score: 32; achieved ~35 in 2024.
- Consumers and end-users (KfW-only, due to business model): focus on non-discriminatory access to financing for education, home ownership, and energy-efficient housing; legal basis in KfW Law (Art. 2), bylaws, and ministry mandates. Sustainability guideline for domestic business and KfW’s human rights policy apply. No 2024 cases of non-compliance with UNGPs/ILO/OECD guidelines and no severe human rights incidents linked to consumers/end-users.
- Engagement and feedback: ongoing customer satisfaction measurement via KfW new customer monitoring (≈1,000 sub-borrowers/month) and NPS for housing programmes; additional input from financing partners and bank associations.
- Actions for consumers/end-users:
  - Education financing: KfW Student Loan (own risk, broad eligibility), Education Loan (on behalf of BMBF with Federal Office of Administration), and the optional loan component under the Upgrading Training Assistance Act (Aufstiegs‑BAföG). 2024 promotional volume for these three products: EUR 172 million.
  - Housing security: loans for owner-occupied property (Home Ownership programme, incl. options without energy-efficiency conditions) and cooperative housing (loan for cooperative shares). 2024 promotional volume for housing security: EUR 2,354 million. Key product volumes reported for 2024 include Home Ownership (EUR 5,266m), KfW Student Loan (EUR 244m), Upgrading Training Assistance (EUR 125m), Cooperative housing (EUR 25m), and Educational Loan (EUR 13m).
- Accessibility: commitment to accessible digital services per BITV; annual accessibility statement updates; 2024 comprehensive BITV audit, continued testing through at least 2025, ongoing monitoring via dedicated tooling, and proactive internal/external audits.
- Targets and performance: customer satisfaction ambition 75–80% (top‑2 on a 5‑point scale) across private and commercial customers; KPI methodology and governance outlined. Latest value (31 Dec 2024): 66.1%, with shortfalls driven by external factors (interest rates, federal budget, funding availability, sustainability requirements). Continuous dialogue with clients to improve financing conditions.
- SDG alignment: education products contribute to SDG 4; housing-related products to SDGs 7, 11, and 13; non‑energy‑efficiency home ownership supports SDG 11.
- Corporate customers/SMEs: SMEs face structural financing barriers (information asymmetries, limited credit history, small ticket sizes). DEG and KfW improve access via SME credit lines and on‑lending through partner banks, with product information, marketing support, advisory via KfW’s Infocenter, monetary incentives for concluded financings, concessional loan features (below-market rates, long tenors, fixed rates, repayment bonuses), and risk-sharing with on‑lending banks in selected programmes (e.g., start-ups).

nodes.title: Customers – Corporates
nodes.heading: 7.3.3 Customers – Corporates
nodes.start_phrase: Corporate customers have been identified as an additional company-specific material topic due to the particular nature of KfW Group’s business model.
nodes.summary:
- Customer satisfaction performance and measurement: KfW set a 75–80% “top-2 box” ambition for overall customer satisfaction (question: “How satisfied are you with KfW’s services overall?” on a 5-point scale). The KPI is a simple average of weighted averages for commercial and private customers, calculated monthly from representative samples in key domestic programmes. As of 31 December 2024, the result was 66.1%, below target. Shortfalls are attributed to external volatility affecting promotional products (interest rates, funding availability, federal budget developments, higher market rates, increased sustainability requirements). KfW engages in specialist dialogue with clients to make financing conditions more customer-friendly. New customer monitoring informs Strategy 2029 and user-centric product, process and service development.

- SDG alignment: KfW’s sustainability mission supports the 2030 Agenda. Education financing contributes to SDG 4 (Quality education). Housing-related products contribute to SDGs 7, 11 and 13, with non–energy-linked home ownership products supporting SDG 11 (sustainable cities and communities). Further detail is in the SDG mapping of financing activities.

- Corporate customers/SMEs as a material topic: SMEs face structural disadvantages in accessing finance due to information asymmetries, limited credit history, and smaller ticket sizes, leading to higher costs and constrained capital supply—challenges that are particularly acute in developing and emerging economies. DEG supports SME access via bank credit lines. Within KfW’s on-lending model, SMEs access promotional products through their regular banks; KfW supports this with partner information/marketing, monetary incentives per loan, and advisory via an Infocenter trained to guide applicants. KfW loans feature below-market rates, long maturities, fixed-rate periods, and potential repayment bonuses; selected programmes include risk-sharing to ease access (e.g., start-up financing).

- Tracking SME access and strategic targets: One Strategy 2029 aim is for products “relevant to the SME sector” to exceed 40% of total domestic commitments. In 2024, the SME share was 35%, below target, due to a high EU reference rate limiting state-aid–compliant promotional opportunities (impacting SME Bank & Private Clients and Customised Finance & Public Clients) and higher private housing volumes diluting the SME share. 2024 commitments relevant to SMEs: SME Bank & Private Clients EUR 13.4bn (37%), Customised Finance & Public Clients EUR 1.0bn (2%), KfW Capital EUR 1.6bn (100%); total EUR 16.0bn, SME share 35% (with noted adjustments).

- Complaints and grievance mechanisms: Complaints on promotional products are handled by the Infocenter, responsible specialist divisions, and a group-wide complaints management team, which evaluates critical feedback systematically. Group-wide grievance channels exist for all stakeholders, including subsidiaries, to uphold the Code of Conduct and human rights policy. KfW emphasizes a strong risk culture, monitored via a biennial risk culture index in the employee survey; after each survey, an action group defines measures for continuous improvement.

nodes.title: Complaints management
nodes.heading: 7.4 Complaints management
nodes.start_phrase: KfW Group has established grievance mechanisms and channels that are available to all stakeholders to ensure that the policies, actions and targets of KfW Group described above are implemented and monitored effectively, and that human rights, particularly with regard to the Code of Conduct and the human rights policy, are respected.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on KfW Group’s SME financing objectives and performance: target for SME-relevant products to exceed 40% of domestic commitments by 2029; 2024 SME share was 35%, below target.
- Reasons for shortfall: high EU reference rate under state-aid rules constrained SME promotional opportunities (e.g., corporate environmental financing in SME Bank & Private Clients and SME-relevant Customised Finance & Public Clients products), while stronger private housing financing (e.g., Climate-friendly Construction, Federal Funding for Efficient Buildings) diluted the SME share.
- Breakdown of SME-relevant commitments (2024): SME Bank & Private Clients EUR 13.4bn (37%), Customised Finance & Public Clients EUR 1.0bn (2%), KfW Capital EUR 1.6bn (100% of its commitments), total EUR 16.0bn equating to 35% SME share; figures reflect classifications and adjustments excluding specified non-recurring federal measures.
- Customer focus: ongoing measurement of customer satisfaction via the KfW new customer monitoring programme using monthly representative samples; complaints received through the Infocenter, specialist divisions, and a group-wide complaints management system.
- Risk culture: emphasis on responsible risk handling anchored in the Code of Conduct; biennial risk culture index from employee surveys with action groups defining improvements.
- Grievance mechanisms: group-wide channels for human rights and environmental concerns based on KfW’s policy statement and human rights strategy; multiple access routes (verbal, written, email, online forms, in-person with ombudsperson); anonymous reporting via compliance whistleblowing system.
- Ombudsperson: external lawyer serving as confidential contact for suspected legal/compliance violations (corruption, fraud, money laundering, Banking Act, LkSG); screens reports, forwards to relevant Compliance unit without revealing identity; cases handled with impartiality, objectivity, and confidentiality; information available in multiple languages; consumers/end-users informed via Infocenter; no standard method to gauge awareness/trust among value chain workers and consumers.
- LkSG (Supply Chain Due Diligence Act) implementation: coverage of procurement and banking operations; Compliance department operates a central evidence unit, governance framework, and training; Executive Board holds overall responsibility; grievance mechanisms aligned with LkSG, all relevant grievances included in group-wide risk assessments; whistleblowers protected from retaliation; group-wide LkSG complaints procedure documents and assesses reports and aims to acknowledge receipt within seven calendar days.

nodes.title: KfW Group’s grievance mechanisms
nodes.heading: 7.4.1 KfW Group’s grievance mechanisms
nodes.start_phrase: The group has established procedures to respond to complaints and reports of potential human rights-related and environmental risks, and to react appropriately to any of its own breaches of duty.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and basis: KfW Group outlines its grievance mechanisms for human rights and environmental risks and breaches of duty, grounded in its Human Rights Policy Statement and strategy.
- Access channels: Complaints can be made verbally, in writing, by email, via online forms, or in person to the ombudsperson; banking-related complaints may go directly to the relevant business sector; employees and third parties can report potential criminal offenses anonymously via the compliance whistleblowing system.
- Ombudsperson role: An independent external lawyer serves as a confidential contact for suspected compliance violations (e.g., corruption, bribery, fraud, money laundering) and breaches of the German Banking Act and the LkSG.
- Case handling by ombudsperson: Reviews reports for company relevance and forwards substantiated matters to the appropriate Group company’s Compliance department without revealing the whistleblower’s identity.
- Compliance processing: Each Group company has its own compliance organization; KfW Compliance acts as an overarching function for unassigned cases, conducts due assessments, coordinates actions, and pursues legal steps if criminal conduct is indicated.
- Safeguards and transparency: Processing follows principles of impartiality, objectivity, and confidentiality; whistleblower protection details are provided in Governance information; multilingual system information and contacts are published on the Group website; consumers/end-users are informed via the Infocenter.
- Identified limitation: There is no standard method to verify whether value chain workers, consumers, and end-users are aware of or trust the grievance structures.
- LkSG governance: The Executive Board assigned Compliance to run a central evidence unit and a Group-wide governance framework and policy for LkSG obligations, covering risk monitoring, due diligence compliance, documentation, reporting, and employee training; the Executive Board holds overall responsibility.
- System alignment with LkSG: Grievance mechanisms were reviewed and adapted to LkSG; all environmental and human rights grievances are reported to the central evidence unit and fed into Group-wide risk assessments; the whistleblowing system meets LkSG standards and protects against retaliation.
- Complaint workflow under LkSG: Upon receipt, complaints are assessed for human rights/environmental relevance, documented internally, and whistleblowers receive acknowledgment of receipt within up to seven calendar days.

nodes.title: Ombudsperson
nodes.heading: 7.4.2 Ombudsperson
nodes.start_phrase: The group has appointed a lawyer from an external law firm to act as its ombudsperson.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and purpose: KfW Group operates grievance mechanisms to address complaints and reports of potential human rights and environmental risks, as well as its own breaches of duty, grounded in the Group’s policy statement and human rights strategy.
- Access channels: Complaints can be submitted verbally, in writing, by e-mail, via online forms, or in person to the ombudsperson; banking-related complaints can go directly to the relevant business sector; employees and third parties can report potential criminal offences anonymously via the compliance whistleblowing system.
- Ombudsperson: An independent external lawyer serves as a confidential point of contact for staff and third parties to report suspected legal violations (e.g., corruption, bribery, fraud, money laundering), including breaches of the German Banking Act and the LkSG. The ombudsperson assesses relevance and, if applicable, forwards cases to the relevant Group company’s Compliance function without revealing the whistleblower’s identity.
- Case handling and governance: Each Group company has its own compliance organization; KfW Compliance assumes an overarching role if a case cannot be assigned. Investigations and complaint handling follow principles of impartiality, objectivity, and confidentiality. Legal steps are taken where evidence indicates criminal conduct.
- Transparency and accessibility: Information on the whistleblowing system, including whistleblower protections, is provided in multiple languages on the Group website. Consumers and end-users are informed via the Infocenter. The Group notes there is no standard method to verify awareness or trust in these mechanisms among value chain workers, consumers, and end-users.
- LkSG complaints procedure: The LkSG’s minimum requirements apply to procurement and banking operations. The Executive Board has tasked the Compliance department with a central evidence unit and group-wide governance to monitor LkSG obligations, conduct risk monitoring, ensure due diligence, maintain documentation and reporting, and train relevant employees; the Executive Board retains overall responsibility.
- Integration and protections under LkSG: Grievance mechanisms were reviewed and adapted to LkSG requirements. All environmental and human-rights-related grievances are reported to the central evidence unit and included in group-wide risk assessments. The whistleblowing system complies with LkSG and protects whistleblowers from retaliation.
- Complaint processing under LkSG: Upon receipt, reports are assessed for human rights or environmental relevance, documented internally, and acknowledged to the complainant within a maximum of seven calendar days.

nodes.title: KfW’s LkSG complaints procedure
nodes.heading: 7.4.3 KfW’s LkSG complaints procedure
nodes.start_phrase: The statutory minimum requirements set out in the LkSG currently relate to procurement and KfW’s banking operations.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Excerpt from KfW Group’s Combined non-financial report (Social information) detailing grievance and complaint mechanisms.
- Grievance framework and access:
  - Based on KfW’s human rights policy statement and strategy.
  - Multiple channels: verbal, written, email, online forms, in-person with ombudsperson; banking complaints can go to the relevant business sector.
  - Anonymous reporting for employees and third parties via the compliance whistleblowing system.
- Ombudsperson system:
  - External lawyer as confidential point of contact for suspected legal/compliance violations (e.g., corruption, bribery, fraud, money laundering, German Banking Act, LkSG).
  - Assesses relevance, forwards to the appropriate Group Compliance unit without revealing identity; KfW Compliance acts if no specific company can be assigned.
  - Processing adheres to impartiality, objectivity, and confidentiality; multilingual information available; consumers/end-users informed via the Infocenter.
  - No standard method to measure awareness/trust of value chain workers, consumers, and end-users.
- LkSG (German Supply Chain Due Diligence Act) complaints procedure:
  - Applies to procurement and banking operations; Executive Board responsible overall.
  - Compliance department runs a central evidence unit, sets governance and group-wide policy, monitors risks/due diligence, manages documentation, reporting, and training.
  - All human rights/environmental grievances reported to the central unit and integrated into risk assessment.
  - Whistleblowing system protects against retaliation; governed by group-wide LkSG complaints procedure.
  - Process: acknowledge receipt within 7 days; triage and assign; engage with complainant as needed; provide written outcome; feedback within 3 months or interim updates if longer.
  - Annual/ad hoc reviews of actions and the complaints procedure’s effectiveness; 2024 review found no issues.
  - Central evidence unit advises specialist departments and oversees risk management, safeguards, and controls; informed of outcomes and remedial/preventive measures.
- Compliance and risk management:
  - MaRisk requirements protect complainants from disadvantage; ensure effective procedures and controls; annual/ad hoc monitoring.
  - Complaints received outside Compliance must be forwarded to the responsible Compliance unit.
- Communication and training:
  - LkSG complaints procedure communicated via intranet campaigns.
  - Mandatory, documented group-wide LkSG training every two years to raise awareness and enable early identification/reporting.
- Employee-specific channels:
  - Employees can raise issues with managers, workers’ representatives, and HR; complaints rerouted to competent divisions as needed.
- Anti-discrimination (AGG) complaints:
  - Employees in Germany can report discrimination under AGG to a dedicated Complaints Office; employers define the procedure; information on intranet.
  - Mandatory AGG training every three years for KfW, KfW IPEX-Bank, and DEG employees in Germany.
  - Case handling is individualized; complainants control information sharing and actions; subsidiaries (DEG, KfW IPEX-Bank, KfW Capital) have their own AGG offices.
  - Two discrimination cases reported in the reporting year.

nodes.title: Complaints channels for employees
nodes.heading: 7.4.4 Complaints channels for employees
nodes.start_phrase: In addition to the overarching channels already described, group employees can approach their managers with concerns and complaints at any time.
nodes.summary:
- Describes KfW Group’s complaints and whistleblowing process, including routing to a competent unit that clarifies facts, engages with whistleblowers/complainants when needed, and provides written feedback within three months (or updates if longer is required).
- Outlines governance under the German Supply Chain Due Diligence Act (LkSG): annual or ad hoc reviews of due diligence measures; the central evidence unit (within Compliance) acts as regulator and advisor, oversees risk management, and develops safeguards and control measures.
- States that the effectiveness of the complaints procedure is reviewed at least annually and on an ad hoc basis; the 2024 review found no issues.
- Details the Compliance function’s role under MaRisk, including protection against disadvantage for complainants, implementation of effective compliance procedures and controls, and centralized forwarding of LkSG-related reports to Compliance.
- Explains communication and training: LkSG procedures introduced via intranet campaigns; mandatory, documented group-wide LkSG training every two years to raise awareness of human rights and environmental risks and enable early detection and reporting.
- Lists employee complaint channels: managers, HR partners, workers’ representatives; complaints raised elsewhere are forwarded to the relevant division.
- Provides discrimination reporting under the AGG: dedicated AGG Complaints Offices at KfW, KfW IPEX-Bank, DEG, and KfW Capital; mandatory AGG training every three years; complainants control information sharing; no standardized case procedures due to case-specific handling.
- Reports two discrimination cases in 2024, both closed without monetary obligations.
- Notes case handling support: HR documentation and analysis, access to social counsellors and an external psychosocial hotline, and designated contacts for equal opportunities and disability inclusion.
- Clarifies workers’ representation frameworks: Staff Council under BPersVG at KfW and Works Councils under BetrVG at KfW IPEX-Bank and DEG; responsibilities include monitoring legal compliance, receiving and forwarding complaints/suggestions, and promoting gender equality; regular meetings with HR and management to operationalize participation rights; emphasis on dialogue for amicable solutions.
- Describes group-wide complaints management in the banking business: sector- and issue-tailored mechanisms aligned with BaFin minimum requirements and the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights.
- Outlines access points for external complaints: phone, post, email via a publicized grievance mechanism; each complaint processed with relevant departments; complainants informed about arbitration and out-of-court options; affected communities are directed to local partner project mechanisms; focus on accessibility for vulnerable groups.
- Explains monitoring and learning: quarterly evaluation of complaints with key findings reported to the Executive Board; recurrent issues trigger targeted actions and cross-departmental solutions to improve service.
- Notes customer inquiries are handled by specialist divisions or complaints management teams.
- Clarifies that, for value chain workers, it is not standard to refer employees of financed companies or on-lending banks to the financing bank’s grievance mechanisms.

nodes.title: Group-wide complaints management in the banking business
nodes.heading: 7.4.5 Group-wide complaints management in the banking business
nodes.start_phrase:
Grievance mechanisms are in place throughout the group; they are tailored to the individual business 
sectors and types of complaints.
nodes.summary:
- Employee complaints and support: HR documents and analyzes cases; external social counselors and a psychosocial hotline available. Internal contacts include the Staff Council, Works Council, equal opportunities officers, and representatives for employees with disabilities, with open consultation hours and intranet listings. In 2024, two cases were closed with no monetary obligations.
- Workers’ representation and legal basis: In Germany, employees can submit suggestions/complaints to workers’ representatives at KfW, KfW IPEX-Bank, and DEG. Activities are grounded in the Federal Personnel Representation Act (BPersVG) and Works Constitution Act (BetrVG). Regular meetings occur between staff representatives, HR, and management; processes ensure participation rights. Emphasis on dialogue and amicable solutions.
- Group-wide complaints management: Sector-specific grievance mechanisms aligned with BaFin minimum requirements and the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights. Multiple channels (phone, mail, email) with information on arbitration/out-of-court options. Preference for local, project-related mechanisms for affected communities; focus on accessibility for vulnerable groups. Quarterly evaluation of complaints with key findings reported to the Executive Board to address recurring issues.
- Compliance function: Independent unit assesses complaints for compliance relevance and handles potential criminal matters.
- KfW Development Bank: Open-access grievance mechanism (email, online form, branch offices, project managers) with published criteria and reports. Projects must establish local grievance mechanisms per World Bank ESS10 and ESS2, including worker mechanisms. Process includes validity checks, preliminary review, remedial actions, and alternatives if needed; evaluation for systemic improvements. Planned inclusion of anti-retaliation measures; mechanisms are monitored and improved via training and awareness.
- KfW IPEX-Bank: Additional complaint channels (email, web form) for regulatory matters per BaFin and WpHG; acknowledgment with typical processing under two weeks; centralized coordination; option for anonymity. Sustainability-related concerns handled by the sustainability officer and Group Communications. Borrowers must maintain grievance procedures; documentation and training as needed.
- DEG: Grievance mechanism for those adversely affected by DEG-cofinanced projects; written submissions via form/email/post. Independent Expert Panel (IEP) of three external experts decides on arbitration or compliance reviews, ensures alignment with DEG guidelines and human rights policies, and monitors agreed actions. Anti-retaliation policy in place; EU Whistleblowing Directive relevant; no additional training beyond the mechanism.
- KfW Capital: Central complaints management via post or email; anonymity possible. LkSG-relevant matters routed to Compliance. Cross-entity complaint forwarding established. Due diligence checks that VC funds have whistleblowing mechanisms for employees and potentially externals (e.g., portfolio company staff).
- Governance and compliance culture: Code of Conduct anchors corporate values (ethics, integrity, collaboration, risk culture, diversity, leadership, skills). Strict adherence to laws/regulations on anti-corruption, AML/CFT, sanctions/embargoes, securities/tax compliance, data protection, and risk management. Whistleblower protections aligned with EU Directive 2019/1937 and the German HinSchG; safeguards per Section 25h KWG. Participation in Transparency International and EITI; cooperation with BMZ on corruption prevention and integrity standards.
- Cultural development: “Cultural journey” project launched in January 2024 to align culture with strategic goals and enhance employer attractiveness. Employee-inclusive design with workshops; target culture defined with leadership; implementation underway across departments, coordinated by HR and Corporate Development.

nodes.title: Promoting and further developing the corporate culture
nodes.heading: 8.1.1 Promoting and further developing the corporate culture
nodes.start_phrase: KfW Group’s Code of Conduct is at the centre of promotional activities and an expression of corporate culture.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on KfW Group’s governance and compliance framework, anchored in a group-wide Code of Conduct that promotes ethical behavior, integrity, collaboration, risk culture, diversity, effective leadership, and skills development.
- Compliance as the foundation of corporate culture: adherence to statutory, regulatory, and internal requirements covering anti-corruption and fraud, AML/CFT, sanctions/embargoes, securities and tax compliance, data protection, and risk management.
- Alignment with international and national standards: anti-bribery aligned with the UN Convention and German law; whistleblower protections per EU Directive 2019/1937 and the German HinSchG; safeguards per Section 25h KWG.
- Group-wide compliance guidelines supplemented by company-specific policies and work instructions; anti-corruption and crime prevention embedded in the sustainability program.
- External commitments and partnerships: member of Transparency International; DEG supports the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative; cooperation with BMZ and application of BMZ integrity quality criteria in international financing; rules of conduct aligned with German Federal Government and major banks.
- “Cultural journey” project (launched Jan 2024) to strengthen culture in support of strategy, increase agility, and enhance employer attractiveness; co-led by HR and Corporate Development with broad employee involvement, workshops defining target culture, and bank-wide implementation launched at the management conference.
- Governance and accountability: Executive Board holds overall compliance responsibility; subsidiary management ensures implementation; Executive Board delegates group compliance to an independent Compliance department.
- Compliance department roles under MaRisk: early identification of legal changes, decision preparation, monitoring compliance; focus areas include crime prevention, AML/CFT, sanctions, securities, tax, data protection, and MaRisk compliance.
- Designated officers within Compliance: fraud officer (leads crime prevention), money laundering officer, securities compliance officer, and data protection officer; Legal Affairs supports on legal processes; group rules on criminal offense prevention and handling gifts/invitations.
- Reporting and whistleblowing mechanisms: internal and external parties can report suspected unlawful conduct to the fraud officer or an external ombudsperson; integrated with broader complaints management.
- Incident handling: fraud officer logs and processes cases; losses recorded in Risk Controlling’s database; coordinates investigations and risk analyses; can convene a cross-functional fraud task force for exceptional cases (e.g., employee involvement with ≥ EUR 1 million potential loss or major reputational risk); informs the Executive Board; Internal Auditing reviews procedures.

nodes.title: Strategies relating to aspects of business conduct policies
nodes.heading: 8.1.2 Strategies relating to aspects of business conduct policies
nodes.start_phrase:
The prevention of criminal acts and compliance with the Code of Conduct are the collective responsibility 
of KfW Group.
nodes.summary:
- Governance and compliance framework:
  - The KfW Executive Board holds overall responsibility for compliance; subsidiaries’ managing directors and their compliance units implement binding rules.
  - An independent Compliance department, aligned with MaRisk, leads group-wide compliance, early detection of legal developments, decision preparation, and monitoring of regulatory adherence.
  - Focus areas include prevention of criminal acts, anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing, sanctions/embargoes, securities and tax compliance, data protection, and MaRisk compliance.
  - Designated officers (fraud, money laundering, securities compliance, data protection) sit within Compliance; group-wide guidelines govern criminal offence prevention and handling of gifts/invitations.
  - Legal Affairs supports Compliance on legal procedures (e.g., searches and seizures).

- Code of Conduct:
  - Applies to all employees, managers, Executive Board members, and subsidiary management.
  - Executive and subsidiary boards maintain their own codes referencing duties to supervisory bodies.

- Reporting, whistleblowing, and incident handling:
  - Multiple reporting channels (fraud officer and external ombudsperson) are available to employees and external parties.
  - A protected whistleblowing system ensures confidentiality; the ombudsperson (bound by legal privilege) discloses identities only with the whistleblower’s consent.
  - Information and training on whistleblower protection are provided internally.
  - The fraud officer logs and processes all suspected incidents, with losses recorded in a Risk Controlling database, prepares risk analyses, coordinates investigations, and can convene a cross-functional fraud task force for exceptional cases (e.g., employee involvement with loss potential ≥ EUR 1 million or material reputational risk).
  - Executive Board is informed on case handling; Internal Auditing reviews procedural compliance.

- Audits, oversight, and consequences:
  - Annual audit of compliance implementation accompanies the consolidated financial statements; the auditor’s report is submitted to BaFin.
  - Violations may lead to fines and sanctions.
  - Compliance units are included in Internal Auditing’s regular audits; further results are referenced in the risk report.

- Anti-corruption controls:
  - Annual risk analysis under Section 25h KWG identifies and mitigates internal and external fraud/corruption risks, notably in lending/approvals, procurement, and contracting.
  - Two corruption-related cases in 2024 involved external bidders (not KfW employees); those bidders were excluded from the award process per internal rules.
  - Group-wide rules and a Code of Conduct set binding standards for accepting/giving gifts and benefits, including approval options and fixed value limits, emphasizing transparency and conflict-of-interest management.

- Training and culture:
  - Annual divisional discussions on anti-corruption are required.
  - Mandatory e-learning on criminal acts, AML/CFT, and data protection; targeted in-person training for higher-risk roles (e.g., award/approval functions and foreign branches).
  - Cultural change initiatives (“Cultural journey”) are communicated via workshops and events.

- EU Taxonomy (Article 8) disclosures:
  - Presentation of Taxonomy KPIs, including the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) stock and flow, with associated coverage over total assets and percentages of assets excluded from GAR numerator/denominator in line with Article 7 and Annex V.
  - Additional disclosures on trading book, financial guarantees, assets under management, and fees/commissions (with methodological notes on use of turnover vs. CapEx KPIs for counterparties and general lending).
